let us hand out the bouquets to others who are probably more deserving of them. Let us hand them out—verbal bouquets though they be—to those Chinese who, as the Hon. Mr. Holyoak reminds us—and reminds us from his own vital experience—have been loyal and proved their loyalty in different directions, all of a practical nature. This section of the community deserves all that has been said of it. It has had to surmount. those inborn feelings of sympathy which come naturally, if unreasonably, when the actions of our nationals are the subject of discussion or rebuke. The national life is akin to the family life. Attack the one, and the members of it fall into either a defensive or offensive line. It is more than likely that in throwing in their lot with the British for either business or sentimental reasons, those who have earned for themselves the right to receive Mr. Holyoak's commendation, retain decided opinions as to the claims of China to be heard on such questions as extr-territoriality, Concessions, etc.; and the desire to have happenings at Shanghai and Shameen probed by an impartial board. If they do not, we shall be inclined to throw doubts on their possession of any sense of loyalty to anyone, and to say that they are merely of that class of opportunities which, of the Machiavellian, are the most Machiavellian. But those who have set themselves the task of assisting in the fostering of trade; the return of the workers, and a desire for right feelings as between foreigners and Chinese, give us confidence that British administration, justice, freedom, education, etc., have not been in vain, and that the fruits of these things are to be seen in this desire of a large and influential body of Chinese to recreate confidence and to set in motion again the wheels of finance and commerce. The two

Chinese Unofficial members of the Legislative Council have been mentioned; and we are glad that this has been done. Their position is no sinecure, and especially so at the present moment when doing good by stealth and without the flourish of trumpets is part of their daily work. Of the work of Dr. S. W. Tso it is difficult to speak adequately, for it has not necessarily been called into play by the frolic of the moment but by a deep seated belief in the principles that have made British justice the envy—and, as in the present instance—the hate also—of different parts of the world. In this particular matter it is good to remember that many realise we are all in the same boat, even if, as Mr. Douglas Jerrold would any, not necessarily with the same skulls!

headline: STRIKE BREAKERS.
text:
The stream runs dry, or, in other words, health, comforts, and advantages are seldom fully appreciated until they are lost. At the present moment too many of Hongkong's residents are aware of this truism, and to give instances would be both superfluous and irritating. However, bad though conditions have been for the past six weeks, a little consolation may be gained by the reflection that things might have been worse, Happily there has been no rationing of food, and for this fortunate state of affairs we owe a deep debt of gratitude to the Dairy Farm Company. Lack of space forbids us to go into details about the great amount of extra work being done by the depleted staffs at all the branches and in all departments of that essential organisation, so we shall merely give a few facts about their main shop at the top of Wyndham Street. From enquiries made a "China Mail" man learned that about thirty-five of the forty-two Chinese employees there walked out six weeks ago. Five of the faithful six were in the shipping department, and there they have remained during the strike. The other thirty-five clerks, butchers, sausage-makers, tripe-cleaners, picklers, pie-makers, bacon-curers, and coolies—downed tools and disappeared at the nod of the "dare to dies." To add to the troubles and worries of the few European employees the closing of the markets sent hordes of Chinese and others, who do not at other times patronise the place, up to the "Ngao Nei Xung Si." On the first day of the strike a Portuguese lady who, we understand, assisted there during the 1922 strike, took up her former position at the cash desk. She has been there every day since from 10 a.m. During the early morning spell, 7 a.m.—9 a.m., a Jewish gentleman and his wife act as cashiers. On the second day of the strike two well-known Queen's College masters walked into the shop and offered their services....They were received with open arms by the frantic staff and given jobs straight away, and every day for the past six weeks they have been at their posts from 7 a.m. till after closing time. Later on another master from the same school came to help. Further assistance has been rendered by several young ladies from the Italian Convent who come in relays of two at a time. Behind the scenes two mariners, a hefty soldier, and a Filipino, "Samson," have been doing a lot of heavy work. So little time have the regular employees and voluntary male assistants to spare that breakfast and tiffin are "bolted" on the premises. For the first three weeks of the strike the three butchers, Messrs. Bradbury, Blackley, and Bertram, were working on the premises from 5 a.m. till 8 p.m., while the acting secretary, Mr. Thompson, installed a bed in his office in order to be there day and night. The much needed services of an assistant butcher were obtained during the third week, but even then the strain on the butchers was tremendous. Considerable relief was given to the overworked staff by the re-opening of the markets a fortnight ago. However, even now with fewer customers and more coolie labour, it is still impossible to supply cooked stuff, while sausages, corned beef and dripping can only be prepared at spasmodic intervals.

Our reporter was greatly surprised at the amount of work performed there behind the scenes from 6 a.m. till 5 p.m. shipping orders, hotel orders, club and hospital orders, Shameen and Cheung Chau orders, splitting up frozen carcasses with mighty cleavers, branch orders, etc., etc. As he said: "What would we have done without the Dairy Farm?"

Should your piece of beef or mutton not be the cut you specially like or what you have been in the habit of getting from the Dairy Farm Company, remember it is strike time, consider the long hours these butchers are working, and in your hearts render thanks to the overworked men of Pokfulam, Wyndham Street, and East Point Ice Depot.

headline: REPRESENTATIONS TO BE MADE.
text:
The tightness of the money market formed the chief subject of discussion at a meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce yesterday afternoon.

The Chairman, Mr. Li You-chuen, said his attention had been drawn to the fact that owing to the property slump, many banks had suspended connection with their clients. His personal opinion was that considered generally the tightness of the money market could hardly be avoided but things might, however, be improved if proper arrangements were made with the compradores of the Banks. It had been suggested that one of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council might be requested to approach the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, the managers of the Banks and others in order that satisfactory arrangements might be made.

The meeting eventually agreed to appoint members in connection with such negotiations; Mr. J. M. Wong to represent the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Mr. Mok Ching-pong to represent the banking circle (Mr. Ho Sai-wing, the compradore of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, having previously declined to serve).

In the course of further discussion it was stated that a contributory factor in the bringing about of a tightness of the money market was the prohibition on free movement of goods and it was agreed that the Government should be requested to consider permitting the export of goods which represented the lifeblood of the Colony.

A unanimous decision was also passed emphasising that the strike was caused by intimidation carried out by a small section of the labouring community and did not represent the wishes of the merchants.

headline: PROPAGANDA.
text:
We can only ascribe the absence of a serious system of propaganda in the present condition of affairs, to an innate sense of modesty on the part of the British executive, or those who might well consider the matter of effective propaganda. In ordinary circumstances it can only be the small-minded who can find satisfaction in lauding its own virtues and chronicling its own achievements. The British characteristic of coldness and aloofness excludes all idea of "the puff direct." Hongkong might well have dinned—and continual dinning of facts is the success of all propaganda as it is the success of advertising—into the obstute minds of those who are willfully blind and refuse to think of its virtues of administration; its educational facilities; its laws which do not differentiate between rich and poor—the lowly ricksha-puller and the lordly merchant; its gifts to famine

nfested districts; and its humane conditions of factory employment. The list is admittedly brief as it is meant to be. That has not banged the big drum of self-advertisement is as it should be and as British people would have it. But there comes a time, as in the present distress, when the question of propaganda takes foremost place: when the question of counteracting untruth—to mention only one of the great evils—should become very vital. Its vitality at the moment does not seem very evident. The Colony has suffered to a considerable extent by reason of the fact that the uncontradicted untruth has had free play, even though evidence of the eyes should have convicted lying statements of their falseness. The people of this Colony have not starved; the harbour has not been blockaded; and there have been no signs of terrorism. It may be that the intelligence of the coolie, labouring, and amah class, has been under-rated; but it is surely evident that if peace is to be our portion in the future, the aim must be to free these people from a bondage of fear, and a belief in what may be described as "fairy tales," that, as we have seen, has hitherto reacted so disastrously on our fortunes. There has been no harsh criticism of the Government's handling of a somewhat complex matter. It has had good will and hearty co-operation of an unstinted kind. But we may be permitted a word to suggest that whilst it lost no time in appointing officials to control food supplies and labour, it should have lost no time in appointing a Director of Publicity or Propaganda, to feed the foreign and Chinese Press—with information—to placard the Colony with refutations of silly rumours; to present the facts of any case that may be, in no uncertain light of language; to "feed" outlying places with information; and

amongst the many things such a Director or a Bureau under his charge could do, would be to make use of such natural avenues of publicity as the tried, tested, and most effective method of the cinematograph. It is not too late to introduce such a necessary system as we have here indicated. The "China Mail" are this has suggested that there should be a Publicity Bureau as part of the Government's organisation. The present need merely proves that the suggestion was not an idle one.

headline: The Penalty of Personality.
text: Mr. Lloyd George when he became Chancellor did not abandon the expression of his views about dukes, and on these views the flames of party feeling/fed. On the other hand, from the moment Mr. Churchill went to the Treasury he seemed to put out of his mind his authorship of the famous taunt: "Is Labour fit to govern?" and that he had ever delighted a bored House with his brilliant interventions in debate at the expense of Labour or Russia, or whatever happened to be in his path at the moment. It is well known that he was profoundly grateful to Mr. Baldwin for the demonstration of confidence which his appointment to the Treasury carried with it, and he has obviously aimed at being the most "urbane of Ministers. But just as one does not forget the Lloyd George of 1905 and 1909, so it is evident that a section of Labour in particular cannot forget the Churchill of more recent years. Thus we had back bench Opposition murmuring during the Budget speech Mr. Churchill ignored them, though irritated, and did no more than turn on one of his own supporters who interrupted him. Then when the Chancellor had listened to three days' criticisms of his proposals and sought to reply, he was shouted down by the same back bench element and had to abandon his speech. Unless he has indeed been transformed, a Churchill does not tolerate very much treatment of this nature, and if a dead-set is to be made against the Chancellor, the old fighting spirit will inevitably come out. Conservatives will back him to a man, and the new Parliament may easily be split from top to bottom by controversy at a time when the leaders of all parties desire an earnest and co-operative handling of current problems. It is in this last fact that the best hope of avoiding undue controversy lies.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
STRIKE COMMENCES TO-DAY.

PREMIER'S GREAT EFFORTS.

The coal situation is regarded in Ministerial circles this afternoon as of the gravest, but not as hopeless. Mr. Baldwin is doing his utmost to make the parties confer, impressing upon them that a strike must be averted.

Mr. Baldwin' conferred first with the coal owners and secondly with the miners, after which representatives of both sides made statements to the Press indicating that neither side had made a concession.

The Miners' representatives, after seeing Mr. Baldwin, conferred with a special committee of the Trade Union Congress. Afterwards these conferees joined a conference of all the Trade Union executives.

headline: Trade Unions Decision.
text: At a meeting of the Executives of all the Trade Unions at Westminster it was unanimously and whole-heartedly decided to assist the miners, including financial help in the form of a levy from each district.

headline: Handling To Cease.
text:
A special committee of the Trade Union Congress and Railwayways' Transport Workers' Union executives, ordered the handling of coal to cease at midnight on Friday (to-day).

All coal then railed is to be placed in the nearest siding which may exclusively be used for coal-ing engines, but not passed to other depots. No imports may be handled.

headline: Premier's Statement.
text:
Mr. Baldwin, in the course of a statement to the Miners' Federation, summarising the negotiations during the present position, specifies the Owners' concessions as the principle of a minimum wage and the inclusion of August profits in wages; and the suggestion of the relaxation of the Seven Hours' Act to enable an offer of better wage terms.

The Premier also sets out the Federation's refusal to accept wage reductions or relaxation of hours, and points out that the Federation offered not the slightest contribution to the concessions.

He emphasises that the Government is not prepared to subsidise the industry.

The foregoing was issued shortly prior to the intimation that Mr. Baldwin would not make a speech in the House of Commons to-night, which had been announced. The postponement is due to his meeting both the parties to-night.

Earlier in the evening the situation was discussed at a special Cabinet meeting.

headline: German Crisis
text: The glut in coal is causing a crisis in German industry. Ten million tons lying in the Ruhr must be sold at any price to save the industry from ruin. The only method of disposing of it is by export. This explains the refusal of the German delegates to the International Miners' Federation in Paris to join the British miners in their strike or even to support the transporters who are preventing export. The coal situation is such that Ruhr owners are resorting to wholesale dismissals. Negotiations, in which the chancellor is participating, are proceeding in Berlin to solve the problem.

headline: OFFICIAL STATEMENT
text:
A statement issued by the Ministry of Labour after midnight says that following a meeting of the Cabinet yesterday, evening, at which full consideration was given to the whole circumstances of the coal dispute, the Prime Minister had a further conversation with the representatives of the miners and the owners.

The miners told the Prime Minister that they desired to co-operate in the proposed enquiry with a view to a full investigation of the methods of improving the productive efficiency of the industry for the purpose of increasing its competitive power in winning markets. They intimated that it was not fair to require a reduction in wages with the present cost of living before an attempt, by means of an enquiry, to secure a contribution

toward meeting the difficult situation with which the industry is confronted.

The Prime Minister consequently announced that the Government was prepared to assist the industry until next Spring, when the enquiry will be completed.

The Prime Minister requested the owners to suspend the notices for a fortnight in order that the necessary discussions might proceed concerning the way in which temporary assistance could be afforded.

A statement issued by Mr. Cook on behalf of the miners, says that a settlement has not yet been reached.

A further meeting with the Prime Minister was arranged for noon to-day after Mr. Baldwin met the owners.

The mine workers will receive their instructions immediately after to-day's meetings.

headline: PEKING LEGATION. / ADEQUATE SAFETY ASSUMED.
text:
In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. H. W. Looker (formerly of Hongkong) Mr. Ronald McNeill (Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs), said that he had not received the official report of the Soviet envoy at Peking.

There was a loopholed wall at the Legution, and it could safely be assumed that the British Charge d'Affaires had taken all possible steps to ensure the safety of the British Legation.

headline: TROUBLE SPREADING.
text: The bank strike is spreading. The employees of the Credit Lyonsnais have followed the lead of the Banque Nationale de Credit in demanding 100 francs monthly increase against an offer of 45 francs. They went in procession twice to the bank buildings, but were dispersed by the police. Two other banks employees have come out and those of the Gomptoir Desompte strike to manage

headline: FACING FACTS.
text:
The Premier is urging employers to take their employees more and more into consultation regarding routine and management.

London, Juhe

Before an audience of 50,000 people, a speech was made by Mr. Stanley Baldwin at a victory rally at Welbeck Abbey, in which the Premier appealed for an all-round increase of ten per cent. in industry. Mr. Baldwin pointed out with pleasure that his appeals for an industrial truce had resulted in the men of both sides sitting down together and facing realities as never before.

headline: FATAL OPIUM CLASH
text:
Press reports state that General Li Kwei-yuen, Chief of Staff of the First Mukden Army, was killed and Cheng Quo-jui, Commandant of the twenty-eighth Brigade and Yuen Shi-fu, Chief of the Martial Court, were seriously injured yesterday afternoon, following a disagreement during a conference in an upper story of the Mukden Headquarters in Chapel suburb, Shanghai.

It appears that General Chang Tsung-chang, Tupan of Shantung, sent Cheng Que-jui to Shanghai to investigate the local traffic in opium. A disagreement arose between Yuen Shi-fu and Li Kwei-yuen, whereupon the latter's body-guard fired, wounding Yuen, whose bodyguard returned the fire wounding Cheng. Li Kwei-yuen jumped out of a window and broke his neck.

According to anti-opium circles, a large quantity of opium reached Mukden headquarters on Friday evening.

headline: ARMED RAIDS
text:
Five armed desperados entered a bank in the Chicago suburb of Cicero, herded the thirteen employees into a back room, scooped up $10,000 and escaped in a motor car.

Later in the day a party of men, possibly the same gang, entered a large jeweller's store in the business part of the town and by similar tactics secured loot valued at $20,000.

headline: BACK TO GOLD.
text:
The Federal Reserve Board has published the details of a plan whereby American financial interests support Britain's in the maintenance of the gold standard in Britain. While there were actually two distinct transactions, one being the establishment of a direct credit of $100,000,000 to the British Government by Messrs. Morgan and Company, the statement deals with the arrangement between the Bank of England and the New York Federal Reserve Bank prior to the reestablishment of the gold standard and the abolition of the ban on gold exports from Britain.

Other Federal. Reserve Banks are also participating in the creation of a credit of $200,000,000 for the Bank of England upon which it can draw if conditions require.

The Reserve Bank undertakes to sell gold on credit to the Bank of England during the next two years, but the sum if not exceeding $200,000,000 shall be outstanding at any time. The credit, as far as used, shall bear interest at one per cent, above the Reserve Bank's discount rate with a minimum of four and a maximum of six per cent., or, if the Federal Reserve discount rate exceeds six, then at the rediscount rate of the bank. Interest payable by the British Government on credit established is determinable in a similar

When the Bank of England purchases gold equivalent to its deposit in pounds sterling, which shall be recorded to be credit of the reserve banks, it may be used in the purchase of eligible commercial bills which the Bank of England shall guarantee, and the discount earned on such bills shall be applied to the payment of interest.

Simla, June 1.—The Persian and Baluchistan border has been in a disturbed condition for some time. The latest reports show that the Persian garrison at Khwash is besieged by Persian and Baluchistan tribes and has already suffered heavy casualties.—Router.

headline: “RED” MAGIC.
text:
Home

In spite of the Home Office edict that foreign delegates should not be allowed to attend the Glasgow Red conference there were present a German, and a French Communist.

The Chairman, Mr. Pollitt then introduced the second foreign delegate, the French Communist Mdle, Laval, who like Dr. Stocker, was spirited away after delivering an address.

Sir William Joynson Hicks, the Home Secretary, whose ban was described by the Reds as childish and absurd.

Half an hour elapsed. before the Pressmen were allowed to leave the Hall.

The Communist leader Mr. McManus apologised for detaining the Pressmen but declared the Government was responsible.

In the House of Commons last week in reply to questions, Sir William Joynson-Hicks, the Home Secretary, "intimated that permission had been refused to various foreign Communists to attend the Communist conference at Glasgow on May 30. Any of them landing without permission would be deported."

Mr. George Lansbury and Mr. J. R. Clynes asked the definition of "subversive propaganda" and whether the Government had decided that Communist propaganda was illegal.

Sir William Joynson-Hicks replied that certain things were permitted to British nationals but the Government could not permit foreigners to come here and do them (Ministerial cheers.)

Mr. Lansbury asked if this was the result of communications with other governments with a view of preventing Britons participating in international conferences abroad.

Sir William Joynson-Hicks replied that there had been no international arrangements and that this action had been taken without reference to any other Governments.

Teheran, June 1.—The Mejlissh has passed a law granting a sole Government monopoly for the export, import, purchase, sale and warehousing of tea and sugar. The Government will levy a duty of two "krans" on sugar and six "krans" on tea respectively.—Reuter.

headline: SPIRITED AWAY.
text:
There was an enthusiastic and dramatic scene at the Communist conference at Glasgow when it was announced that in spite of the Home Office ban on foreign Reds, Dr. Stocker, the fraternal German delegate, was present.

Dr. Stocker went on the platform amidst tremendous enthusiasm and the singing of the "Internationale."

He declared it was childish and absurd of Sir William Joynson Hicks (the Home Secretary) to think he could stop the British revolution by endeavouring to prevent the Communists of different countries from meeting.

headline: TSINGTAO TROUBLE.
text:
This afternoon, the Tokyo Labour Union representatives visited the Foreign Office and presented a copy of a resolution which had been passed at a mass meeting in support of the Tsingtao strikers and demanding the "suspension of armed intervention, refraction from threatening the Chinese Government, and the punishment of the blindly selfish Japanese capitalists."

The Government, replying, emphasised that the warship was not sent for the purpose of strike suppression, but for protecting the Japanese residents from probable riots owing to the Chinese inability to do so.

headline: HELD UP:
text:
INCIDENTS AT SHANGHAI

Shanghai: July 7.

The shipping situation remains the same and the concentrated intimidation of the last few days resulted in a number of tramwaymen failing to turn up this morning, but the Tramway Company is determined to carry on. Specials guarded the trams to-day. There was no incident. Otherwise, however, the situation is quiet, though forty thousand are out of work due to the cutting off of the bulk of the power supply of electricity. In many cases resumption is believed to be taking place owing to the inadequate dole which is being given out.

The bulk of the power supply of electricity has been discontinued. A number of mills are installing their own motors.

Agitators are taking advantage of the discontinuance of the electricity supply and are furthering unrest, but no serious trouble has occurred.

The intimidation of tramwaymen is being carried on without abatement. Last evening, a crowd of a hundred, including a number of former tramwaymen, held up a car conveying thirty tramway fitters from the repair shops. They forced the fitters to accompany them to Chinese territory.

About half the telephone operators have resumed work.

The body of an American member of the crew of the s.s. President Pierce has been found in a creek, whilst a British blue-jacket has been missing for sixty hours and has not yet been found.

At the inquest on the man who was shot by the American seaman Dizik, it was stated that the deceased was shot by the sailor when the latter was protecting a Municipal officer. Two men who were arrested were charged at the Mixed Court, one for inciting to riot and the other for firing crackers. The first was remandied on bail, and the other nominally fined.

The Japanese community is raising subscriptions for the purpose of making a presentation to the Volunteers and naval landing parties in recognition of their services. So far, nearly ten thousand dollars have been subscribed.

headline: Chungking Unrest.
text:
A wireless message from Chungking, dated July 6, says the Japanese concession was surrounded by a crowd all day long. The Japanese Consul considers that a collision is likely. The authorities have not taken effective action.

Reports from Hoihow and Pakhoi'say Chinese gunboats are expected to arrive shortly.

Ningpo is reported quiet. The local authorities are prepared to provide protection.

headline: Dosser Trial.
text:
Shanghai; July 7..

The Mixed Court dismissed three of the four charges against Dosser who was allowed bail on Tls. 20,000 security (which the Soviet Trade Mission is alleged to be furnishing).

Dosser, was remanded for a week. All charges against his wife were dismissed. The remaining charge against Dosser is that he made preparations to openly incite disorder.

The Court dismissed the charge that accused was making preparations to commit a hostile-act against certain foreign states, because the text of an article in the Chinese Criminal Code, whereon the charge was based, meant "declare war" and not "hostile act." Two other charges were dismissed as they rested upon the above mentioned charge.

headline: Diplomatic Halt.
text:
It is admitted in Legation circles that negotiations with the Chinese, with regard to Shanghai are at present at a standstill, but the opinion prevails that Mr. MacMurray's arrival will probably produce development in a day or two.

(Mr. MacMurray is the newly appointed U.S. Minister to China who has left Shanghai and arrived yesterday at Tientsin).

headline: THE STRIKE.
text:
JIONG KONG'S EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.

Elsewhere in this issue (says the "Shanghai Mercury" of July 1), will be found an extract from a private letter received from Hongkong under date of June 21. We would particularly commend this article to the careful perusal of our readers. There can, we think, be little doubt that the Governor of Hongkong is acting with the full approval not only of all foreign residents in the "Colony", but also of all foreigners in this country. The policy of the Hongkong Government can only be regarded as an excellent example—an example which the local Authorities would do well to follow.

There is of course, a certain amount of difference between the Shanghai and Hongkong cases. That of Hongkong was brought about solely by the inischievous activities of the Kuomintang Reds. As Sir Reginald Stubbs pointed out at last week's meeting of the Legislative Council, there is nothing to discuss or adjudicate or on which to compromise. There is no shadow of grievance to justify this strike. In regard to the Shanghai incident, it will be readily admitted that there was something to discuss. It must also be admitted by Chinese and foreigner alike that the interested Powers took prompt action with a view to settling the affair. Six delegates were sent down from "Peking-fully empowered to come to terms, but the Chinese persisted in demanding matters entirely irrelevant to the incident of May 10, with the result that the foreign delegates did the only thing possible—they returned to Peking. The question of these irrelevant matters and also that of the Nanking Head affair will be settled in the course by the responsible parties in Peking. Neither have any legitimate hearing upon the present state of affairs in Shanghai, and neither have any claims upon the attention or consideration of China's school boys, and others responsible for prolonging the strike.

After practically a month of dislocated commerce it seems to us that some concerted action should be taken by the foreign employers. There can be little doubt that the strikers have been led to believe that their employers will pay them strike pay. Is it to be seriously thought that any soldier-minded tapan would agree to such an action? We think—and certainly hope—not. Such being the ease, is it not tim that the attitude of the employers was made known. Surely such a step would expedite the return to normal conditions, but foreigners must follow Hongkong's example and present a united front. Any dilly-dallving would be fatal, but we are firmly convinced that the time has come when the foreign employers should make known their attitude.

The following is part of the letter quoted by the “Shanghai Mercury”:—

'You will already know that Hongkong is in the throes of another disgusting strike. The Government is determined this time to fight to a finish, and we have no Prince of Wales' coming to prepare for. Already the Chinese have asked to be taken back, but the Government is going to decide that matter. It will be a case this time. May I and will you take me back? You must have read of the drastic action already taken by the Government, and honestly, I am proud to be under the Union Jack here. We can and are showing the Chinese what we can do. No money exceeding $5 can be taken away from the Colony, no rice, no flour, and practically all foodstuffs are strictly forbidden to be exported. The Chinese are already feeling the 'pinch,' but the Europeans have plenty to eat and drink. No rioting or disturbances of any sort have arisen, and the military have charge of the whole situation. Thousands daily are going to Canton, but what they think they are going to do with $5 and shortage of rice in Canton, remains to be seen.

headline: CUSTOM'S. DECLINE.
text:
Reuter learns that owing to the Shanghai strike and other disturbances and unrest all over the country, the net Customs revenue for the six months ending on June 30 declined by 1,500,000 taels compared with last year, out of which there was 1,000,000 taels decline during June. It is considered, however, that the decrease need not cause undue alarm to bondholders.

Washington, July 8 It is announced that Mr. Kellogg has appointed Mr. MacMurray and Mr. Silas Strawn Layer as America's Commissioners at the Shanghai Customs Conference.

headline: FUNERAL
text:

headline: AS OTHERS SEE US.
text:
A FIGHT TO A FINISH.

The Red wing of the Kuomintang who are again in control in Canton five chosen to make war on a neighbouring and friendly Colony, says the "Peking and Tientan Times" of June 20. There is no other meaning attaching to the "spontaneous" outbreak of the strike and other disturbances which followed the return of the Reds to authority in Canton. Whilst the whole of China was in an uproar, and anti-foreign demonstrations had occurred in such distant centres as Chungking, Hongkong remained normal and quiet. But within a few days of the re-establishment of the Reds in Canton all was changed. The strike, fomented and engineered by the Canton Government, and the unprovoked attack upon the Shameen, form the culmination of a long series of provocations during the past two years. The Governor of Hongkong has expressed his determination to "see this thing through." We are

"See this thing through. We are confident that the entire British community are with him to a man and to a woman in their will relentlessly to prosecute this struggle to a victorious issue."

The sermen's strike and the manner of its Termination have taught us all a bitter and unforgettable lesson. There can be no discussion of terms this time. As Sir Reginald Stabbs publicly declared at a meeting of the Legislative Council: "There is nothing to discuss or adjudicate, or on which to compromise." It must be—a fight—to—a finish.—There is "no shadow of a grievance" to justify this strike. It is purely political in complexion and hatched in malice and ensoy by the Kuomintang Reds. The demands published by the agitators who have brought about this crisis are essentially political. The Chinese have some reason to complain of the refusal to give them representation on the Shanghai Municipal Council. It was a counsel of perfection, not of higher wisdom and tact, which denied the Chinese this participation in the administration of the "Molel Settlement." It will unquestionably be remedied when reasonable conciliation on our side is commended by a similar spirit on the part of the Chinese, and when the acceptable compromise regarding representation of foreign taxpayers on the Municipal Council of the ex-Russian Concession in Hankow is adopted in the case of similar foreign areas in "Tientsin," in accordance with an undertaking that has hitherto been utterly ignored.

But in Hongkong the Chinese have no such grievance. The demand for the popular election of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council is inadmissible while a similar right is denied to the British and foreign community. There is no discrimination. The British community have been conducting a perfectly legitimate campaign for a limited electoral representation during the past few years. They have of course, not sought to enforce their demand by disorderly processes. If and when their desires are met probably similar rights will be conceded to the responsible section of the Chinese taxpayers. But at present we are all on the same basis in the principle of representation. The Chinese members of the Council have always been high-minded and able men, and truly representative of the Chinese interests. That is more than can be said of the self-styled authorities in Canton. If there were a genuine popular election in that city nothing would be more certain than the overwhelming repudiation of the Kuomintang extremists. It is a characteristic feature of Chinese inconsistency in their disputes with the foreign authorities, that they demand rights under foreign auspices which they do not enjoy, and apparently do not even make any serious attempt to acquire in their own country. The Chinese taxpayers have absolutely no voice in the administration of the native city of Shanghai; and even the inchongta and futile effort to secure the popular election of a Tupan after the civil war soon died out of initiation. What voice have the Chinese taxpayers got in the municipal administration of the native cities of Peking, Wuchang, Tientsin.

For very many years the relations between Hongkong and Canton were of the most cordial description. There was no common recognition of the essential unity of interests, and the one co-operated with the other in a fine spirit of mutual helpfulness. The Semmen's Strike, openly supported and sustained by Dr. Sun Yat-sen's administration in Canton, by whom the strikers were housed and fed and subsidised, was the first really serious breach. With the exception of a brief interval the relations between the two Governments have been progressively worsening. This most deplorable break with the past is the solely to the intrigues of the Polshevists and to the amazing influence which Moscow's agents came to exert over the left wing of the Kuomintang. While Red Army instructors have been imported and have played a large part

in the military campaigns since Sun Yat-sen returned to Kwangtung in 1923, the Hongkong Government has been reviled for its sympathy with the great commercial class. It has been accused of subsidising the revolt against the appalling exactions and tyranny of the Red regime in Canton. But this may be said for the Colony. If it had lent British officers to Chen Chiung-ming or to Chan Tim-pak, and had actually given them financial and other support, if it had actually turned its very natural and proper sympathy for the sufferers from Red rule, in Canton to active help of the opponents of that regime, and backed the moderate section of the Konfrontung against Hu Hun-min and his gang, it is safe to say that the Canton Bolsheviks would not be where they are today. If it is right for a section of Chinese political extremists to accept the aid of one Power, why should it be improper for those with real material interests,—the merchants, not the politicians—to seek and to be granted the help of another?

But in point of fact we have not given material aid to anybody so far. We have scrupulously maintained our traditional policy of non-interference, in the face of intense provocation, though in the many crises that have arisen during the past two years as the result of the appalling military situation in the province, when the Red Kuomintang's late hung by a thread, a slight departure from that neutrality would have decided the issue. What would the Soviet have to say if Chang Tso-lin imported British or Japanese officers into Harbin? There would not, merely be a protest. There would be another concentration of Red troops on the frontier. We have not even protested against what is unquestionably things being as they are, a deliberate-ly Fostile action. If the British or Hongkong Governments wanted to interfere they could do so, and to some purpose. If they wanted to associate themselves with the Yunnanese they could transport not 600 but 6,000 troops by sea from Yunnan and turn them loose within striking distance of Canton, and they could keep them in power. They could do the same in the case of Chen Chiong-ming, who has apparently re-taken Swatow. We are becoming tired of these preposterous and childish charges of interference. It is inducing a feeling of exsperation, and that attitude of mind which is a temptation to do the very things we are wrongfully accused of doing. If we lent a handful of officers, money and munitions, to Chen Chiong-ming, and rendered him a little unobtrusive. Naval support, he would have no difficulty in cleaning up Canton. Such help has undoubtedly been solicited on many occasions by one or other of the factions hostile to the Kuomintang extremists, and the fact is that such overtures have always been refined. Could we have a more convincing pretext than the attack on the Shameen and the officially-inspired plot against the Hongkong Government if we really wished to interfero.

Finally, let us quote the tribute paid to the British Administration in Hongkong by Sun Yat-sen when he was about to resume power in Canton in February, 1923:

“The difference between the Governments in China and Hong Kong impress me so much that I begin to wonder why the British

could do so much on the barren rock of Hongkong within 70 years. China during a thousand years has been unable to accomplish the same things as Hongkong. In the administration of Hongkong corruption is the exception and purity the rule. On the contrary, in China corruption is the rule. In China we have not got a Government. We have been misgoverned for many centuries. You (the Hongkong University students) must learn the English example, and we must carry the example of good Government to all parts of China. That is the best advice San Yatsen has ever given to his countrymen. In its fulfilment the Hongkong Government are undoubtedly prepared to offer any assistance that may be welcome, and that does not involve us in a breach of the policy of neutrality. Even in the present crisis, though the British have been provoked beyond measure, that policy will be and should be maintained. But we hope that the Kuomintang will take warning from the situation their avowedly and consciously hostile policy has produced, and will forthwith cease from further provocation, lest they make desperate remedies inevitable. We shall continue to defend our lives and property on the Shameen, but we shall go no farther unless Hu Han-min, and his fellow-despernades forces us to abandon our neutrality and to intervene, as the only means of self-preservation.

headline: Deudlock Continues.
text: A message from Peking states that deadlock between the Powers and China continues, the former insisting on discussion in the first place of China's demands relative to the Shanghai disorders, while China desires to discuss, simultaneously, the revision of the Treaties and other demands which the Powers consider require a larger conference.

headline: FIVE DEMANDS. / ORDER OF PRECEDENCE LEADS TO DEADLOCK.
text:
The situation continues a deadlock. While nothing has been officially announced it appears that the Chinese Government desires that negotiations regarding the last eight of the thirteen demands, as well as the revision of the so-called unequal treaties shall be taken up simultaneously with the first five demands. It is understood that the Powers insist that the five demands arising directly out of the Shanghai incident be discussed first. Meanwhile agitators continue to urge negotiations with Britain alone.

The Chinese Chamber of Commerce has hitherto handed to the bureau distributing strike pay $620,000 but it is believed that it is insufficient to last much longer.

headline: ORDER TO TROOPS.
text:
TO AVOID BOLSHEVIST PROPAGANDA.

According to the Ching Pao, Feng Yu-hsiang has issued an an order to the troops directing them to avoid Bolshevist propaganda and to oppose it to the utmost, pointing out that Kalgan is on the borders of Mongolia and Russia, but that there is a vital difference between the habits and customs of the Chinese people and those of these countries and, moreover, the national spirit differs. He concludes by urging the Chinese to adhere to the teaching, and practices of their own ancient sages.

Russian aeroplanes, it is reported, are arriving here to-day. The Finance Ministry has been requested to provide $20,000 for the reception of the aviators.

The Secretariat of the Chief Executive, it is reported, has sent a circular by telegram to the provinces saying that the Government has maintained a firm attitude from the beginning in regard to the Shanghai affair. A popular movement based on patriotism is to be commended, but the actions of bad characters, such as the destruction of the homes of foreigners, is to be avoided as it will be prejudicial to the progress of the negotiations. It concludes that henceforth the popular agitation must be carried on by peaceful means only.

headline: CHINA'S DISORDERS.
text:
HOME PAPERS' STRONG COMMENT.

Contemplating a long struggle, with not a few complications, the Times, in a leader, expresses the opinion that the time has come for British policy toward China to take a clear and definite shape, and declares that if this policy leads to effective common action so much the better, but the responsibility for defining threatened British interests dies first and foremost with the British Government.

The Times considers the British are now hampered by past neglect, particularly in allowing the Washington decisions to remain in cold-storage, but the fact of the stimulation of anti-British agitation may be the outcome, directly of indirectly from the report of the Commission of Enquiry into the Shanghai disorders.

The paper emphasises the necessity of a clear renewal of British initiative and adds that the situation is intimately connected with the recent discussion of the cruiser programme. We must be unfettered in the disposal of means whereby British nationals and trade in the Far East can be continually protected.

headline: Bungled”？
text:
The "Daily Telegraph" diplomatic correspondent says there is a strong feeling among certain members of the Cabinet about the manner in which the proceedings, relating to the Shanghai incidents in regard to the action of the British police there, have been "bungled, to perhaps the serious detriment of British prestige," and adds that the anxiety of a section of the Diplomatic Body, whether through undue nervousness or for reasons connected with their countries' material advantages, to placate the Chinese agitators is indeed regrettable.

The writer suggests that a British veto should from the first have been placed upon the foreign project of a "Diplomatic investigation" to be carried out in an atmosphere of Chinese intimidation, and adds that firmness on the subject is needed in London and is likely to be forthcoming, judging by the recent statements of Mr. Austen Chamberlain and Mr. Samuel.

headline: Loyalty To Verdict.
text: 'The Observer says that the British Government's view of the Shanghai troubles is that a final and impartial authoritative verdict should be pronounced at the earliest opportunity. There may be a case for a new International enquiry, and in any case Britain will welcome a verdict and will loyally abide thereby, whether or not involved in the censure or dismissal of any British official.

headline: ARBITRATION. / U.S. WOMEN AND THE WORLD COURT.
text: Supporting the attitude of President Coolidge, the National League of Women Voters has announced its disapproval of any possible eleventh hour reservations with regard to the Protocol for the establishment of a world court of arbitration when the Senate takes up, in December, the question of American adherence to such a court.

headline: KOREA FLOODS / FORTY MILLION YEN DAMAGE.

The damage is estimated at forty million yen.

The casualties include twelve dead.

Singapore, July 13.—A report from Parim states that the Singapore Maru is hard aground and that an attempt to float her at midnight on Saturday failed. The ship must first be lightened and cooler have been sent to that end.—Renter

headline: “ALL POWERS.”
text:
PEKING'S NEGOTIATIONS

SOVIET PLANES.

Yesterday's evening vernacular papers state a proposal was brought forward at to-day's meeting of the Foreign Relations Committee that negotiations regarding Shanghai be with Britain only, but the majority, rejected the proposal and decided that negotiations will be with all interested Powers.

After rejecting the proposal to conduct negotiations, regarding Britain only, the Foreign Relations Committee decided negotiations were to be carried on with all interested Powers.

Three Soviet aeroplanes have arrived from Russia. A fourth aeroplane has broken down en route.

headline: JAIL FOR A BRIBE.
text: A Chinese woman was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday with offering a bribe of $25 to Sergeant Major Li Sze with a view to being released after she was detained in connection with the murder of a man at Lung Cho Ching. The woman's defence was that she gave the money to the detective for safe keeping as she understood that all prisoners had to leave their valuables with the police. The Magistrate imposed a sentence of three months' hard labour.

headline: LUCKY ESCAPE.
text:
ALARMING STUBBS ROAD ACCIDENT.

CAR STRIKES PARAPET.

Mr. H. S. Bennett, manager of the Hongkong Telephone Co., and two friends had a lucky escape from serious injury on Monday afternoon. They were proceeding to the Peak by Stubbs Road when their car met with a nasty mishap. They were approaching the second bend after the hairpin bend when a tyre burst and the car ran into the granite wall at the cliff side. Mr. Bennett was flung violently against the wind-screen but luckily escaped with nothing more serious than a few scratches and bruises. His two friends were thrown from the car by the force of the impact, also fortunately without serious injury. That all three escaped so lightly, when they might easily have been involved in the gravest consequences, was largely due to the fact that the car was travelling at not more than 15 miles an hour.

headline: EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
text:
STANDARD OIL COMPANY CONCESSION.

WAGES COMPENSATED.

The Standard Oil Company of New Jersey has announced the adoption of an eight-hour day in its mid-continental oilfields, also a new wages scale which will partly compensate workers for the resultant loss in wages.

The announcement is regarded as a great boon by the workers as a twelve-hour day has been in force since digging the first well in 1859.

headline: POISON GAS.
text:
RUSSIAN EXPERTS.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. W. Foot Mitchell, Sir L. Worthington-Evans (Secretary for War) said that he had information that Chinese militants had introduced to China German chemists for the purpose of manufacturing poison gas, and employing Russian experts to assist their military plans.

Mr. W. Mackinder (Labour) asked whether some of the Russians were members of Koltchak's army, but, the Secretary for War said that he was not aware of that.

headline: RIOT SEQUEL. / QUESTIONS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.
text:
LABOURITES' TRANSLATION.

Replying to questions by Labourites, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that he had not yet received a full report of the evidence before the Mixed Court at Shanghai in regard to the shootings, nor a report of the Commission of Inquiry.

Mr. W. M. Adamson (Labour) said that Chinese newspapers had arrived in England and a translation showed that an inspector had admitted in evidence that he did not know a warning must be given before shooting.

Mr. Chamberlain was of the opinion that the report to which Mr. Adamson had referred was the report of the commencement of the Enquiry on people who were killed. The mail which brought the commencement of the report had not brought the end of it.

He was of the opinion that he ought to see the whole of the evidence before he expressed an opinion.

Replying to Mr. J. Beckett (Labour), Mr. Chamberlain said that he did not know the exact nature of the divergence in views in the recent discussions between the Diplomatic representatives at Peking in connection with which the French Minister withdrew.

Meibourne, July 15.—Major di Pinedo took off on his flight to Japan but was compelled to re-land owing to a leakage. He will re-start at eight on the morning of July 16.—Reuter.

Paris, July 15.—The National Fête was celebrated brilliantly all over France. Paris witnessed an imposing ceremony at the Unknown Soldier's tomb and the finish of a relay race from Verdun whence runners bearing the symbolic torch came by way of the battlefields to lay the symbol on the grave. In the Moroccan towns impressive military parades took place attended by huge crowds of natives and at Habat by the Sultan with his Viziers Hayes.

headline: CHINESE CUSTOMS.
text:
MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S STATEMENT IN PARLIAMENT.

PUBLICATION OF REPORT.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. H. Day (Labour), Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that the British representatives to the Chinese Customs Conference had not yet been appointed. He was unable yet to say when the Conference was likely to be held, but he pointed out that the Washington Treaty provided that it should meet China within three months of the ratification at a date and place to be designated by the Chinese Government.

Asked whether he was aware that the American Government had already appointed commissioners to the Customs Conference, Mr. Chamberlain said that that did not arise from the question.

Replying to questions Mr. Chamberlain said that the action to be taken on the report of the commission of investigation of disorders at Shanghai was being considered. He was not prepared to publish the terms of the report at present.

Asked whether it was not thought desirable that the report should be published as soon as possible in view of Press reports of its contents, Mr. Chamberlain said that there were limits to the extent to which Governments could be called upon to produce information because journalists surmised what the information would be.

Asked whether it was not possible for other Governments to publish the report Mr. Chamberlain said that he hoped that publication, if it occurred, would be simultaneous in all countries.

headline: “OTHER” "POWERS.
text:
SUGGESTIONS FOR POLICY IN CHINA.

GOVERNMENT CONSULTING.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. W. Forrest (Labour), Mr. Austen Chamberlain reiterated—that the Government was consulting the other Governments concerned in regard to the International Conference concerning China. In the course of the consultations, suggestions in regard to the policy to be adopted had been received from the United States and other Governments and were now being considered.

headline: (FAVOURITE ITALIAN BARITONE)
text: Of course, we could not propagandise exactly on Bolshevik lines. It is not for us, as for them, to exploit destructive tendencies; nor to indulge, as they do irresponsibly; in the money corruption, to which the gross personal venality of nearly all-Chinese politicians and soldiers so readily lends itself. But there are plenty of other openings, which we could utilise if we tried. No nation has better vantage-points in Chinese life, or a larger store of living experience to draw on there. Only our attitude remains too much that of a very old business firm; which is so conscious of selling the best article in the market that it thinks it be-neath its dignity to advertise. We all know what happens to such firms under modern conditions. It is what must happen... (with momentous consequences) to British influence in China, unless we endeavour more systematically, there to meet propaganda with propaganda.

headline: CANTON POSITION. / PROSPECTS OF WARFARE.
text:
General Li Fook-lam, the "governor" of Honum which is on the opposite side of the River to Canton, has, it is stated, forbidden strikers to land in his territory for fear that they may be agents of the Reds, or the so-called Leftists of the Kuomintang party.

Martial law has been declared and is strictly enforced, says the "China Mail" Canton correspondent. To the eye it does not appear as if the Leftists will take up arms against the anti-nationalisation of property clique of whom General Li is said to be a leader with General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief.

No matter what way the trend of politics may be following, General Li has tried to keep the strikers from Hongkong and Shameen at arm's length.

Hongkong verinacular papers report that General Cheung Kai-sleak, now one of the most powerful of the Leftists and the commander of the "Whampoa Cadets" is organising his forces so as to make a clean sweep for Communism. An offensive from Whampoa to Honam is stated to have been planned.

Taking the various reports con- junctively it seems that although the politicians have patched matters up, the militarists are not content to leave important questions in suspense.

Some of the local vernacular papers have also published reports of the alleged taking over of the Kung Yee (Hospital) in Canton by the administration. The Kung Yee is reported to have large sources of revenue and the stated reason for Government control is that the Kwangtung University is to be run in conjunction with the hospital. In one source it is mentioned that the hospital properties are worth about a million dollars. Added significance is given by the return to Hongkong of Dr. S. F. Lee, former superintendent of the hospital.

headline: IN EARNEST. / WHAT STRIKERS ARE LEARNING.
text:
NAVAL YARD EXAMPLE

That employers were in earnest when they warned employees of the dire results to themselves which would follow absorption from work is proved by the fact that they have adhered steadily to that policy and that strikers who have returned or attempted to return have been informed that they must commence again as beginners in their particular class of work.

That many of them were unacquainted with British methods, and imagined that the warning was just bluff, is also proved by the astonishment with which they have received the news of the employers' adherence to their previously announced policy. This has been so in the case of the Hotels Company and the Naval Yard, and doubtless it will be the case when Harbour office employees, coxswains, etc., present themselves for re-employment and this in spite of the clearness with which the Harbour Master made the position clear to them. The Star Ferry workers will also have to start on the lowest scale of wages, and doubtless the same astonishment will be manifested by them.

Of the 200 workers who have returned to the Naval Yard all but a dozen or so have reconciled themselves to the inevitable and have remained in the knowledge that half a loaf is better than no bread. Not all of them, however, will be able to find reemployment just yet even at the lowest scale. In normal times about 2,000 are employed, but the largest number, which can be usefully employed at the moment is 500. Those returning at the Yard appear to be coming in batches of grades, the first being the engine fitters and the next the carpenters, this pointing to some arrangement by which a consensus of opinion of these different branches is taken.

Peking, July 16.—The vernacular papers report that the Waichiaopu has protested to the Diplomatic body recently regarding the Shanghai Council cutting off electric light. Sig. Cerruti is reported to have replied but the nature of the reply is not announced.—Reuter.

headline: GETTING OUT.
text:
STRIKERS EVADE CANTON TICKETS.

ROUNDABOUT ROUTES.

In spite of the activity of pickots in Canton, individual workmen are escaping from the fold and even getting down to Hongkong by circuitous routes, writes the "China Mail" correspondent.

Practically everybody with the appearance of a striker who passes along the Canton Bund is closely examined by pickets in uniform and the first question is "Are you trying to get to Hongkong? If so the person, man or woman, is taken to Strike Headquarters on the second band for "trial."

Although river steamer traffic between Hongkong and Canton has raised up with the exception of the Hong Kong there are still means of travelling. It is reported that pickets are also on duty at Taishatan, the terminal of the Canton-Kowloon Railway, to prevent the rank and file deserting by that route. To circumvent the agitators, smokers have first left Canton by tow-boats which ply to all points in the delta. After reaching an intermediary point "defaults" go on by another towboat to Macao where steamers convey them to Hongkong. The s.s. Anjo and No Chow have been running between Hongkong and Macao this week. It is the same with the railway. Strikers leave by tow-boat for a point near the Boea Tigris Forts, tranship inland and board a train in Chinese territory for Samchun. There is undoubtedly evidence, adds the correspondent, that unrest is spreading, particularly with the cargo coolies who have complained of bad guild management on their own pipt and preferential treatment to flavoured guilds by the

It appears that when the coolies struck sympathetically with the scamer in the last exodus from Hongkong, the same thing happened. At that time seamen were enjoying themselves in flower-boats and having picnies on the river while the coolies had to live in temporary shacks by the side of the Bund. This time, the seamen are alleged to be receiving both meals and "tea-money" while the outsiders' grumble at inferior quarters and irregular food.

headline: STRIKE NEWS. / CHINESE ASPECT IMPROVES.
text:
During the last two days, the number of tea-houses, restaurants and eating houses which have resumed business, has been constantly increasing. Some of the establishments have only a very limited menu, "devoid of variety owing to the absence of cooks who are away, and who find difficulty in getting back.

The majority of native barber hops have also re-opened their oors.

Every day the vernacular press announces new bodies of special guards organised by Chinese communities to assist in preserving the peace. A suggestion has now been made that the district special guards also supervise that part of sanitation relating to the disposal of nightsoil as the poorer classes are not aware of the arrangements made.

Nightsoil coolies are also returning to their jobs especially in the central district and in Yaumati.

Yesterday the Chinese Trade Maintenance Association elected Mr. Ho Kwong as chairman, with headquarters on the first floor of the City Hall. Chinese merchants who experience difficulty in connection with merchandise, transport, etc. are asked to report to the Association, at City Hall, at 11 a.m. each day, and they will be assisted as far as possible.

Brokenhill, N. Rhodesia, July 16.—The Prince of Wales who leaves Capetown on July 29 for South America has completed his programme in North Rhodesia, the main feature of which was the meeting of the native chiefs in all parts of the territory whom the Prince lengthily and impressively addressed. Thereafter the Prince opened the hydro-electric scheme at Mulungushi whereby a narrow river in the heart of Central Africa will be converted into a mighty lake, usable for generating power. The Prince congratulated all concerned in the affair and also acknowledged the courtesy of the Belgian Government in sending the Governor of Katanga to greet him.—Reuter.

headline: U.S.A. IN ACCORD
text:
Reuter learns that the latest indications from America show the United States is entirely in accord with Britain in regard to China. The general line of policy of both is to push on as rapidly as possible the Washington Conference programme when conditions in China are favourable for such a step.

It seems obvious the tariffs Conference will necessarily precede any conference on extra-territoriality and it seems likely that the body which will ultimately deal with the latter will be a committee of preliminary investigation into the circus riots.

headline: SHAMEEN ECHO.
text:
"ACTION LIMITED TO DEFENCE."

Peking, July 17. FACTS OF THE CHINESE CHAOS

The British Legation has given out the text of two further Notes recently sent to the Waichiaopu on the subject of the Shameen incident. The first is dated the 13th and quotes the substance of the Consul-General, Sir James Jamleson's report. It goes on to observe that the deplorable incident has been exploited for the purposes of an unrestrained press campaign of calumny and malice against Britain, the promoters of which, without waiting or caring to learn the facts, have utilised

the touching remarks of Your Excellency and of the honourable senior unofficial member; for I had the honour of serving with the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki on this Council for two fairly long periods, and can also claim a friendship with him which extended over twenty-eight years. The disaster which overtook the Chinese community yesterday was so sudden and of such an appalling magnitude that it still leaves me, who have suffered the loss of many personal friends in it, incapable of properly expressing my feelings. You will know that Mr. Chau Siu-ki was associated with the public life of this Colony for about forty years, and that he had always given to it of his best, unstintingly and without any expectation of reward. During that long period he served on innumerable public and charitable committees, and closely identified himself with almost all movements having for their object the general welfare of the Colony. Though of a retiring disposition, his sterling character, innate good sense, and capacity for public affairs soon won for him a place in the front rank of our public and commercial life. About two years ago he signified his intention to retire from public life, but he never quite gave up interest in all important matters concerning the welfare of the Colony. It was only on the day before the disaster that he attended a meeting in my office in connection with the strike, and another meeting in the same evening concerning the formation of Chinese street-guards. But an inexorable fate struck him down the next morning. I am sure that he himself would have preferred his end, cruel as it was, to being spared to mourn the terrible loss, in one single day, of more than half of those nearest and dearest to him, including his aged mother, two sons and a daughter, two daughters-in-law, two grand-daughters, and his only grandson whose birth last year brought to his yearning heart such unalloyed joy. Though Mr. Chau Siu-ki is no longer with us, he has left behind him the cherished memory of a life full of good deeds well and unostentatiously done—a life which is a fine example to the younger generation. Our hearts sorrow for his death as for the deaths of so many useful and promising lives. On behalf of the Chinese community, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shou-son and I respectfully join in the expression of sincere condolence with the surviving members of Mr. Chau Siu-ki's family, and also with the relatives of the other victims of this cruel visitation. headline: A GREAT LOSS. / TRIBUTES TO THE LATE MR. CHAU SIU-KI. / COUNCIL SPEECHES
text:
Tributes were paid to the memory of the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki at the meeting of the Legislative Council to-day when His Excellency expressed sympathy with those remaining members of the family and with all who had been bereaved as a result of the disaster in the Western part of the town. His Excellency spoke of the long record of good service of the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki who had served for a considerable period on the Legislative Council. He was a citizen who could ill be spared.

Mr. Holywork spoke as follows: Sir.—On behalf of my colleagues

I desire to associate myself with the remarks expressed by your Excellency in connection with the terrible disaster at Po Hing Fong in which our friend and colleague, Mr. Chan Shin-ki, lost his life as well as most members of his family, and to his surviving sons we desire, to extend our deepest sympathy in the terrible tragedy which has befallen his family.

It has been my privilege to know the late Mr. Chan Shui-ki intimately for the last 23 years and of recent years I have served with him in Public endeavour in many ways as well as having been associated with him in this Council, in various committees, and in business affairs. He was a man for whom I had the highest admiration as one who was just and able in his views and an extremely loyal supporter of the Government of this Colony. We, no less than the Chinese, have lost a friend to whom we were deeply attached as well as an enthusiastic and able Representative in connection with all causes for good Truly it may be said the Colony is the poorer for his tragic passing. headline: THE HARBOUR.
text:
STILL MORE SEAMEN AVAILABLE.

HOPEFUL SIGNS.

The s.s. Tung On. which arrived back from Kongnoon yesterday afternoon, sailed for Canton this morning with more supplies. Her trip to Kongnoon was uneventful except that she was aground for some hours on the Wangmun Bar and was not re-floated until H.M.S. Moorhen rendered assistance with the supply of a lighter for emptying the bunkers. Six European passengers were brought from Kongnoon.

Owing to the registration of numbers of seamen, the shipping situation has considerably improved and there will shortly be nothing to hinder ships with cargo to carry, moving from their anchorage. The Hai Ning, of the Douglas Steamship Company, has already done so and is now at her wharf taking on cargo, chiefly American Naval stores.

The harbour is gradually assuming a more normal appearance and many more launches are noticed to be in operation. Engineers and coxswains for the harbour launches have been engaged in considerable numbers and others have applied to the Police for employment. The War Department launches have maintained a service since the beginning of the strike and by an unfortunate coincidence there were mishaps to both this week-end. As a result of going aground at Green Island the Tommy Atkins sustained damage to her bows, part of the stem piece having been torn away. The Umphali has been refloated after having been aground for some days.

headline: MACHINE-GUNNERS' MEMORIAL.
text:
DUKE OF CONNAUGHT'S UNVEILING

The-Duke-of-Comnaught unveiled the Machine Gun Corps memorial in the open space between the Mall gates, and St. George's Hospital, Grosvenor-place, W. on May 10. The memorial, sculptured by Mr. F. Derwent Wood, R.A., shows the bronze figure of David, more than Sft. high, leaning on Goliath's sword. The figure stands on a base of Mazzano stone, and on each side are shown laurel-wreathed machine-guns.

The Duke chatted with four members of the corps who had won the Victoria Cross—Major J. R. N. Graham, Captain A. E. Kerr, Lieutenant W. A. White, and Corporal A. H. Cross—and inspected the guard of honour formed of former members of the M.G.C., now in the Royal Tank Corps.

The Duke recalled that 1,120 officers and 12,671 other ranks of the corps were killed in the war, 2,881 officers and 45,377 other ranks being wounded, missing, or taken prisoner. The casualties were more than a quarter of the total strength. As the National Anthem was played, it was sung by the large crowd. Many women cried, and several relatives of dead members of the corps were helped into St. George's Hospital in a fainting condition.

Hundreds of men and women pressed forward to lay their wreaths besides the larger one sent by the corps, and the police had to link hands to regulate the movement.

headline: J. B. HOBBS.
text:
EQUAL OF BERNARD SHAW OR LL. GEORGE.

LINKS OF EMPIRE.

In an article in the “Daily News,” Mr. A. G. Gardiner writes:—

Hobbs has won a place in the gallery of modern celebrities as the supreme exponent of the whole range of the batsman's art. He could not be excluded from a list of household names, any more than could Bernard Shaw, Charlie-Chaplin,-or-Mr.-Lloyd George.

"He is a real link of Empire. In far-away Melbourne workers pour out in tides to see Hobbs more eagerly than to see a prince of the blood or a victor of the war."

Hobbs is a perfect and matchless artist. He is so easily the finest cricketer of our generation that it is unnecessary to look for a rival. He would have a place in the world's best team without a challenge.

"After the death of his father he set out with his bat to help his mother to bring up his 11 brothers and sisters.

"However bowlers may change their attack, however clever fields-men may be, Hobbs's amazing repertoire of strokes beats them. The world is now watching Hobbs overtaking Dr. W. G. Grace's mighty achievement, and awaits the day when Hobbs will plant his flag higher on the pinnacle of centuries."

headline: TRADE TREATY.
text:
SOVIET AND GERMAN NEGOTIATIONS.

'Moscow, July 19.

The Ganetzky, head of the Soviet delegation which is negotiating the Russo-German trade agreement, interviewed by the Rosta News Agency, said the negotiations are now almost ended. Only a few questions are unsettled. He declared the Soviet agreed to make important concessions but the German Government demanded further concessions while not making a single concession itself; but the appointment of Count Brockdorf Frantzau to represent Germany seemed to prove Germany's realised importance of immediate conclusion of the treaty.

He was sure Germany would soon make concessions and with goodwill the treaty might be signed in a few days.

headline: FRENCH ELECTIONS.

CARTEL GROUP GAIN MANY SEATS.

COMMUNISTS' POOR SHOW.

The elections to the Council General have hitherto resulted in the Left Bloc winning 47 seats, namely 43 from the right and four from the Communists.

The Ministers Demonzie, Schmidt and Duraffour have been re-elected.

Practically the complete election results show Cartel gained 91 seats, of which the Centre lost 86 and the Communists 5.

Elections took place yesterday all over France with the exception of the Paris area for the Conseils Generaux and Conseils d'Arrondissement. 1,127 results are so far to hand out of about 1,500 expected. They show that the Left Bloc had lost one seat and won 66, of which 8 were conquered by Republicans and Radicals, and 43 by Radical-Socialists and 15 by Socialists.

The Conservative and Moderate Republicans have lost a total of 61 seats, and the Communists 4.

headline: PEAK SERVANTS.
text:
DECISION OF LAST NIGHT MEETING

A crowded meeting of members of the Peak Residents' Association, which was thrown open to non-members, was held in the Peak Club last night under the presidency of Mr. G. M. Young.

The Chairman stated that the Committee, after careful consideration, had decided to place three points before that meeting, in respect of domestic servants who had gone out on strike, namely: that no wages whatever be paid for the days on which they were on strike; that on their return nothing be paid in the way of gratuity or "cumshaw" for any service rendered subsequent to their return; and that they be paid for the number of days during which they worked in June.

A lively discussion followed, as a result of which Mr. T. E. Pearce moved, and Sir Henry Pollock seconded, that no wages whatever be paid for June or any subsequent month that the domestic servants were on strike.

It was pointed out during the discussion that a lead in respect of domestic servants had already been given by the newly formed Mid-Level Residents' Association, and it was desirable that the Peak and Nowloon Residents' Associations should come into line.

On a vote being taken, the meeting was practically unanimous in favour of the motion—that June wages be forfeited by the strikers—there being only two dissentents.

headline: CHINA NOTES. / COMMANDER KENWORTHY'S MEMORIES. / "WHEN I WAS A MIDDY."
text:
The present riots and disorders in Shanghai and other cities remind me very much of the Boxer troubles of twenty-five years ago, when I was a young midshipman on the China station, writes Lieut.-Commander the Hon. J. M. Kenworthy, R.N., M.P., in a Home paper.

The Boxers, who are really a secret society for the reform of the government in China, allowed themselves to be diverted into an anti-foreign agitation. It will be remembered that the Legation and the foreign colony in Peking were besieged for some weeks until a combined force under the German General Von Falkenheyn marched to Peking and relieved them.

Most scandalously the foreign detachments were then allowed a free hand to loot one of the richest cities in the East. Some of the soldiers and sailors made fortunes by the sale of the jewels and rich silks and objects of art they looted. But greater fortunes were made by certain hangers-on, with a knowledge of the value of works of art, who purchased from the looters, at very cheap prices, beautiful jade and ivory ornaments, ancient porcelain, and exquisite gems.

One sailer in my own ship became possessed of a really gorgeous string of cmeralds, but a cute American dealer told him they were only glass and paid him ten dollars for gems that were afterwards sold in San Francisco to an American millionaire for £25,000.

One of the men-of-war that played a great part in suppressing the Boxer rising was a British battleship, the Centurion. Her landing parties chastised the Chinese very severely, and her name struck terror for years afterwards up and down the coast of China.

If the present Centurion, which is a modern battleship, could have been sent out to Eastern waters now, I believe her arrival would do more to quiet the troubles than twelve battalions of soldiers.

headline: CHINESE VENGEANCE.
text:
But the Chinese have curious ideas of vengeance. When a Chinaman has been agrieved by a rich man he commits suicide on his doorstep.

It wasn't easy for a Chinaman to commit suicide on the gangway ladder of the Centurion, but every time she came into harbour at Hongkong and went to her accustomed buoy she found a dead baby lying on it. Any amount of patrolling around that buoy did not prevent this gruesome act, and the sailors whose job it was to jump down on to the buoy and make fast the wire rope, afterwards used for securing the chain of the great battleship, became more and more chary of doing so.

Eventually she had to anchor instead of going to the buoy, and arrange for a police boat to clear it of dramatic souvenirs.

Life is cheap in China, and the rich man who is condemned to death is sometimes allowed to buy a substitute. A poor coolie takes his place, and his reward is that he has three weeks of living on the fat of the land, and his family are cared for afterwards.

The strongest trait in the Chinaman's character is his veneration for his parents and ancestors. They are extremely good to the old people, and Chinese sages declare that this is the reason why the race has lasted so long. The tombstones of departed ancestors are looked upon with peculiar veneration, and some of the railways recently built in China have had to be laid out in a zig-zag course, as no amount of bribery, cajolery, or threats would induce the people to allow their ancestors' bones to be shifted.
