headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
The "anti-Japanese" feeling, which has been bitter since the cotton mill strike, had a climax this afternoon, when three hundred young Chinese of the student class marched in procession along Shanghai's main street, distributing anti-foreign and mainly anti-Japanese literature.

Refusing to disperse, sixty were arrested and taken to a police station, where the ring-leaders were picked out. The remainder were released, but refused to depart. Largely reinforced, they severely handled a constable and made a general attack upon the police station. The police ineffectually fired over their heads, and eventually fired point blank, severely wounding ten, of whom six succumbed. Subsequently, thirty were arrested, including two girls.

Disorders also occurred in Chapei suburb. There is much Chinese excitement, but the situation is well in hand.

The Police report states that the anti-Japanese riots were inspired by the killing of a Chinese workman by a Japanese foreman during the recent cotton mill strikes.

Seven of the rioters have died.

The Chinese Press report that in the riots the police took action dispassionately, adding that the Chinese and foreign authorities have the matter in hand and expect the affair to be settled amicably. They do not expect any further trouble.

headline: NINE MEN. / SIRDAR'S MURDER: GANG. / WHO THEY ARE.
text:
The nine men accused of the Sirdar's murder are the two student brothers. Enaiat, two railway shop workers, a carpenter, an engineer, a taxi driver and a lawyer, the former Zaglulist deputy Shafik Mansur and the official Mahmoud Ismail.

[An earlier cable stated that all of the nine persons accused of the murder of the Sirdar have been found guilty. The court will pronounce sentence on the 7th.]

headline: $45,000,000 LOAN.
text:
HE ARGENTINE'S CREDIT

:

The Argentine refunding loan of $45,000,000 with interest at six per cent., offered by Messrs. Morgan's this morning, was over-subscribed in an hour.

Strasburg, June 2.—M. Painleve speaking at a banquet said that the Government will spare no endeavour in order to guarantee financial stability, of which the first condition is security. It Alsace-Lorraine were against threatened, France would engage her existence to defend them. That does not imply a sentiment of militariam, for while unanimously decided to defend her achievements in Morocco, France wishes only to be a good workman, and have a just peace without oppressor or oppressed. But the French people are not blind and must keep their eyes open for certain dreams of domination, and not submit to defeat. M. Painleve concluded hoping the genios of Alsace Toraine would help in arriving at a mutual understanding between France and Germany.

headline: 30,000 OUT. / STRIKE ONLY / SHANGHAI / LATEST ESTIMATE
text: Although Shanghai's troubles do not yet appear to be over it seems that so far the "general" strike is only partial, chiefly affecting the Japanese cotton mills.

headline: MINOR ASSAULTS.
text:
The strike, which is generally only partial, chiefly affects the

ally partial, chiefly affects the Japanese cotton mills, though some of the tramway, electrical and other municipal employees have one out.

It was estimated this evening that 30,000 people are striking. The police have since released the 900 arrested.

Many minor assaults, chiefly against Japanese, are reported to-night.

Further meetings have been arranged for today, at which it is expected resolutions will be passed demanding the restoration of foreign concessions, abolition of extraterritoriality and the Mixed Court at Shanghai, and also of foreign police stations at Shanghai, and the punishment of the police who shot the students — Reuter. Peking, June 2.—The student meetings held yesterday were only informal as the authorities have forbidden formal public meetings for students since the attack on Chang Shih-chao's residence during humiliation, day

headline: TOKYO WATCHFUL.
text:
The Foreign Office is adopting a watchful and waiting attitude in regard to the Shanghai strike, anticipating combined action with the Powerกอะกอะกกอะก

The cabinet to-day decided to instruct the Walchiaopu to draw up a note of protest to the Diplomatic Corps against the action of the police at Shanghai. It also decided to appoint two high commissioners to proceed to Shanghai to investigate the matter. It is believed they will be selected this afternoon.

headline: SOVIET PROTEST. / CHINESE EASTERN RAILWAY. / UNFRIENDLY ACTIONS?
text:
Soviet Government circles are reported to be very perturbed at the Chinese continued disregard of the Soviet demand for the dismissal of non-Soviet officials of the Chinese Eastern Railway.

They also accuse China of exerting anti-Soviet influence, for example in negotiating a lozen with Japan for the purpose of constructing a line from Taoman to Tsitsihar, which is inimical to the interests of the Chinese Eastern Railway.

The Soviet Press reports that the Chinese military authorities have requisitioned 400 waggons for the transport of war material to the Soviet frontier at Pogranitshnaja.

headline: IN GERMANY.
text:
National interest is being displayed in the flying week for light aeroplanes, on which Germany is concentrating owing to the pence treaty restrictions. The contests are divided into three classes: in which the maximum power of engines is respectively 40, 80 and 120 horsepower. Twenty thousand pounds sterling are offered in prices; fifty one started. Immune crowds assembled at the Temptel of aerodrome to witness the first of the five separate circuits, the initial one of which is 695 miles, which thirty five contestants completed. The fastest time was done by an Albatross, monoplane 102 horsepower in 541 minutes. The first back of the maximum 40 horsepower class was a Daimler Mercedes 10 horsepower engine. The air-and-circuits will cover 702

from $40.00

RATEPAYERS' MEETING. Shanghai, June 2.—There was again no quorum at the special meeting of the ratepayers called by the municipal council to vote on the resolutions relative to child labour and the printed matter by-law, the licensing of stock exchanges and the increasing of wharfage dues. The number present was two hundred short of the quorum. The chairman thanked those present for their attendance, adding that he felt sure it was the expression of their confidence in the council in the present difficult situation.

Fifty Italian Marines were landed from the San Giorgio, also Americans from the destroyers, as an advance guard for two thousand sailors and marines who are coming to Shanghai in accordance with instructions from the Legations at Peking. The demands of the Peking Government and Shanghai Foreign Commissioner have had the inevitable effect of stiffening the rioters, and the position is steadily getting worse.

PIANOS by COLLARD, BROADWOOD, ALLISON, KIRKMAN, CROWLEY.

London, June 2—The "Daily News" on the Shanghai riots say that whatever else may be said about the fundamental cause it is too late now to leave China to work out her own salvation alone in view of the country's importance to the rest of the world. The paper endorses the "Times" suggestion for a discussion at the Customs conference.

When the rioters threw the Japanese constable into the creek which was shallow, they continued to attack him apparently intending to drown him, but he drew his revolver and killed one and seriously wounded two, whereupon the attack ceased.

headline: LOANS COUPONS MET.
text:
The “Times” City correspondent notes that the coupons due yesterday in two out of three Chinese loans were met, and an announcement with regard to the third is expected. He says it is to China's credit that despite political disorders, the service of foreign debt is maintained undisturbedly, except in a minor degree, and interest is at present being met on all secured Chinese loans issued in Britain with the exception noted.

London, June 3.—The assertion in Glasgow that Herr Stocker, a member of the Reichstag, did not attend the communist congress but was impersonated by a German resident, is confirmed at Cologne where authoritative Communist circles declare that neither Herr Stocker nor any other German Communist went to Glasgow in consequence of the British official embargo.—Reuter.

Sofia, June 3.—The Government has ordered the demobilisation of the ten thousand extra men which the Ambassadors' Conference permitted to be called to the Colours to deal with the Communist menace. The conference previously rejected the application for suspension of demobilisation. — Reuter.

headline: SHANGHAI RIOTS.
text:
When the Volunteers rushed into the building, they rounded up several hundreds of men, who were escorted to the police-station and searched. No arms were found. The police have released the arrested men.

It is believed that armed rioters escaped through a tunnel under the street to the old "New World" building.

headline: Plans Agley
text:
The rioters who fired on the Volunteers yesterday had taken up strategic positions, intending to fire on ratepayers motoring homeward in large numbers from the special meeting. The early termination of this upset their programme.

The failure to secure a quorum was due to the absence of the Japanese.

The strike situation in the international Settlement is slightly more tense. The fresh food markets and Chinese, shops are closed. The rioters are assaulting and otherwise terrorizing all Chinese remaining in the employment of foreigners; but the French Concession is so far unaffected.

The students again held no public meeting yesterday, but the vernacular papers report various meetings in the colleges at which they made extravagant demands such as the withdrawal and punishment of the British Consultant General at Shanghai, the police who killed the students to be sentenced to death; an indemnity paid to the dead rioters' relatives; the British Government to be made to apologise to the Chinese people, in addition to demands for the return of concessions, etc. It understood that the National University, which usually leads student agitators has decided to strike from today as a protest, and is calling all students to gather there to day for a demonstration against “British Imperialism,” also urging that all economic relations be severed with Great Britain and Japan, and that (Chinese) deposits be withdrawn from (British and Japanese) banks, the banknotes of the two countries not to be accepted and no provisions to be sold to their nationals, Chinese employees to be induced to leave British and Japanese employers and students to leave their schools.

headline: Reaching A Settlement
text:
In connection with the efforts of the Chinese merchants to devise some form of compromise, which will end the present disorders and save the faces of the Municipal Council and students, the “North-China Daily News,” editorially believes that the idea is that the students should withdraw the pickets and declare peace. The matter can be referred to Peking for adjustment. The paper says, however, that any interference by the Waichiaopu should be directed towards the students after the fashion of the order recently issued in Peking, ordering the students back to their classrooms.

“We appreciate the efforts of the Chinese merchants to restore order, but as these efforts are being directed at present, we tell them frankly that they are wasting their time. There is only one way in which peace can be brought back; that is by the unconditional surrender of the students and other agitators”

the present among the strikers are 21 killed and 65 wounded. The defenders have had one man seriously wounded and several slightly.

A foreign woman has died as the result of a blow on the head from a brick thrown when rioters attacked a tram.

Armoured cars were rushed this evening into the Western District, where the rioters are concentrating from Chapel suburb, the Chinese control of which gives the strikers a useful base of operations against the Settlement.

headline: Peking To Investigate.
text:
The Government has appointed Mr. Tsai Ting-ken and Mr. Tseng Tsung-Chien (Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs) as High Commissioner to investigate the Shanghai affair. They are expected to leave for there tomorrow.

The Waichiaopu sent a Note this afternoon to the Italian Minister in his capacity as Senior Minister of the interested Powers, relative to the Shanghai situation. The Note protests against the shooting of the students and requests him to bring the Note to the knowledge of the interested Powers.

The Foreign Office's protest reserves "the right to formulate claims which may result from this deplorable incident, for which the authorities of the International Concession are entirely responsible." The Note requests the Ministers to give "urgent necessary instruction to the Consular Authorities in Shanghai to set at liberty those arrested."

headline: Peking Position.
text:
The students of practically all the Universities and Colleges in Peking are striking to-day, as a protest against the Shanghai affair. They are holding a monster demonstration and parade this afternoon.

The Legation guards are confined to barracks and strong pickets are posted at all entrances to the Legation Quarter. Further Clashes.

Many of the foreigners attacked have been rescued in onlying districts by active patents. Further clashes have taken place in the central districts, in which rooms have been killed or injured, it is known that the casualties up to

and other fisheries. The town exports tea, sugar, coffee, maize, wool hides, skins, Angora hair, etc. There are good public buildings and a wireless station. The place is fortified. The population is 69,000 (92,000 whites and many Indians).

headline: Press Hopeful
text: The Evening News, the only evening paper published to-day, considers the situation is not so grave. No doubt the Chinese are feeling the cutting off of food supplies much more acutely than the foreigners, the latter possessing large reserves of imported foods, while the arrival of troops relleves the Volunteers and Police of the heavy strain of continuous duty. But there does not yet appear any common ground for a compromise. headline: “INSULT TO FRANCE.”
text:
STRONG PROTEST.

For An Apology

"An insult to France" is how a French deputy regards the monument erected in Canton to the Annamite assassin who tried to kill the Governor-General of Indo-China last year.

China.

In the Chamber of Deputies M. Outrey, the deputy for Indo-China, notified Lis intention to interpellate the Government in connection with its protest to the Chinese Govern

ment regarding the monument erected in Canton by Annunite revolutionaries to the memory of the Annamite who threw a bomb at Mr. Merlin, the Governor General of Frida Thiem on June 20 last killing five and wounding eight Frenchmen.

Me: Outrev, in accepting. M. Briand's request for a postponement of the interpolation pointed out. That since the outrage the Government had not obtained from the Chinese Government an apology

or an indemnity. He described the erection of the monument as an insult to France.

M. Outrey also hoped that the Government would take action as regards the Soviet Government in connection with Mr. Karukhan's alleged statement on the morrow of the outrage expressing his satisfaction at its perpetration.

M. Brind replied that if the authenticity of Mr. Karakahan's words could be proved the Government would insist on respect for engagements with France.

headline: "THE KING!"
text:
SHAMEEN'S BIRTHDAY CELEBRATIONS.

Shameen yesterday celebrated H. M. King George's sixtieth birthday as in previous years.

From II. a.m. till noon, the Consul-General was at Home to all friends and the loyal toast was honoured at noon from 12:30 p.m. till 2 p.m.

The Shameen was also at Home to friends and the Consul presided. In the evening, the Consul gave a dinner to the Consular Body, cadets, officers from H.M.'s war ships in port and the Commissioner of Customs. At the Club dancing was indulged in till 2 a.m. with the assistance of a his band from Hongkong. The gunboats in port dressed ship for the occasion

raised by the deputy, and public debate would but impede the normal progress of the pourparers. M. Briand added that it was "as yet unconfirmed that M. Karakhan would have landed the "attempt upon M. Merlin, but if the Ambassador really did so the French Government would insist on a penalty. M. Ontrey said he himself was satisfied.

Earlier this week Deputy Outrey informed the President of the Chamber of Deputies that he would question the Minister for Foreign Affairs what measures have been taken by the French Government in order to protest to Peking concerning the monument erected in Canton by the revolutionaries in memory of the Annamite who threw a bomb at the Governor of Iodo-Chirii, M. Merlin, and in order to demand indemnities for the victims of the criminal attempt.

Hongkong and the whole world was startled by this outrage on the occasion of M. Merlin's visit to Shaneen, after calling here on his return to Indo-China from Japan, M. Merlin was the guest, with members of his staff, at a dinner given by the French community of Canton, at the Victoria Hotel. Shortly after the gathering had sat down, a young Oriental throw a bomb at them from a window. He was pursued and fired at and was seen to have dived into the creek. Subsequently a body confidently believed to have been that of the assassin, was found in the river. It was stated that the assassin who caused the deaths of several French residents and wounds to others, was an Annarnite. A memorial is said to have been erected to his memory by Revolutionaries. Mr. Merlin escaped without injury and came down to Hongkong to aid for Indo-China.

London, June 4—It is now announced that contracts for £3,500,000 have been placed in Britain for two 10,000 ton cruisers and two submarines for the Royal Australian Navy. The cruisers will be similar to the British "County" class.-Reuter.

Sofia, June 4.—The police are very active against the Communists. They arrested 450 person on the ground that they had no identity papers and no fixed occupation. The authorities in Varna have arrested 140 alleged Communists.—Reuter.

√

Lisbon, June 4.—In the Chamber, the Minister for the Colonies explained the reasons for the resignation of Dr. Rodrigues, Governor of Macao. He read a document referring to the works of the port of Macao, showing that the Governor was of the opinion that 60 per cent. of the capital of the company constructing the port works should be Portuguese and the rest divided among British and Chinese. The Governor, who is also a Deputy, defended his attitude.

headline: LABOUR PROBLEMS.
text:
NEW EXECUTIVE COUNCIL ELECTED.

Geneva; June 4.

The Labour Conference has elected a new administrative council comprising the eight States laid down in the Peace Treaty as the highest industrialised countries in the world—France, Germany, Britain, Italy, Belgium, Japan, Canada, and India.

The government group also nominated the Argentine, Spain, Norway and Poland.
The workers' group elected M. Jouhaux for France, Mr. Poulton for the British Empire, Mr. Moore for Canada, Herr Muller for Germany, Mr. Oudegeest for Holland, and Mr. Thorberg for Sweden.

During the Mixed Court trial of alleged rioters in Shanghai a Chinese physician gave evidence that the students were not shot in the back.

A Chinese physician's testimony that the student rioters killed at the Louza station on May 30 were not shot in the back, and the admission of a missionary, who saw the shooting that under the circumstances the police action was inevitable, were the outstanding incidents in the hearing of 19 students charged with participation in the riots in the International Mixed Court before Mr. Jacobs, American Assessor, and Magistrate Kwan. Forty-six students were scheduled to appear, but 27 forfeited bail ranging from $10 to $100.

Dr. O. Fischer watched the case on behalf of the Chinese Commissioner of Foreign Affairs. Mr. E. T. Maitland, police prosecutor, conducted the case against the accused, one of whom was defended by the Chinese lawyer, Mr. Ho Fei. In the afternoon Dr. H. C. Mei was called in to defend some of the students.

The evidence was most important in correcting statements which have been made repeatedly not only by agitators but even by the Peking Government in notes directed to the "Legations. Dr. H. C. Chen, a Chinese physician attached to the Woosung Road police hospital, contradicted the unsupported statements which have been circulated throughout China and in foreign countries that the students were shot in the back. Dr. Chen examined seven of the slain men when they were brought into the hospital after the riots of Saturday and Monday.

Dr. Chen said one of the victims was wounded in the left scapule, the second in the chest, a third in the right side, a fourth in the neck, a fifth in the right shoulder, a sixth in the chest and the left shoulder-blade, and the seventh in the left eye and skull.

The Chinese physician added that any wounds which might have been received in the backs of other wounded men might easily have been received while turning around to beckon the rioters to come on.

Mr. Harry "Westnidge, a Szechwan missionary attached to the China Inland Mission, who has lived for 15 years in China, in giving the evidence, upheld the necessity of the shooting. Near the Town Hall the mob were striking the foreign police with their fists, and witness particularly noticed how forbearing the police were in endeavouring to maintain order. When they were being overwhelmed and had to protect their lives he saw one Sikh policeman draw his baton while the foreign officers drew their canes.

"I noticed," continued Mr. Westnidge, "that when the police had their backs turned to any of the attackers the mob seemed to gather more courage. Crowds from the side street began to flow into Nanking Road. The side of the tram car held up in the vicinity assisted the police in their manœuvres to make a more hurried return to the station. The crowd ran on the other side of the tram in an endeavour to intercept the police, and were by this time rushing forward from all direc

Geneva, June 15.—General Habibullah, the Persian delegate, withdrew from the arms conference owing to the adoption of articles dealing with the supervision of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman which Persia considers derogatory to her sovereign rights and dignity. —Reuter.

tions to the Louza police station. I rather feared what would take place, and suddenly heard the shooting. The police seemed to be inside the entrance, and appeared to come out to meet the throng.

Asked what would have happened if the police had not then opened fire the witness replied:

“I am used to Chinese crowds, and at first this one appeared to be simply the grinning ‘look sees.’ They appeared to be a lot of boys who never expected to run into so serious a matter. I think the students started out without ever dreaming of so serious an ending. If the police had hesitated a moment they would have been trampled down unquestionably.

Cross-examined by the Chinese lawyer as to what nationality he was the witness replied that he was born in England, but that in Szechwan he was called a China-man. After the shooting occurred he rendered assistance to the wounded. The surging mass were yelling so much that he only heard the sound of the shots.

Witness in answer to a question put to him replied by asking the Chinese lawyer if he realised what the students were doing at the time when “they were yelling and screaming and rushing at the police station from three directions in a mixed mob.”

Asked if he would have shot, he replied to the Magistrate that "he would have hated to as a missionary, but that as an officer of the law there was no option. If it had been a foreign crowd at home we would have got the same. I believe that the students were looking for trouble, and not the police."

Witness told the court that some of the older students he saw in the street appeared to be the leaders, and that one man who ran along the side streets shouting and waving a flag appeared to be acting as a warner and a collector of the crowd. Inspector Everson then elaborated the evidence he gave at the inquest, describing how the mob had “made a blind rush at the gates.” When the mob were within six feet of the police he gave the order to fire. The crowd in the opinion of the witness were by no means composed all of students, and by the look of most of them they appeared to be loafers.

The afternoon session was occupied until 6.15 in hearing the evidence of the other foreign police who drove the crowd back to Wing On's and were then attacked near the Town Hall. The case was adjourned, bail being granted to all the accused.

London, June 15.—The considerable anticipations of the Budget duty are reflected in the trade returns for last month, the imports of silk goods totalling fourteen million yards, as contrasted with eight/and a half millions for April. Goods under the category of the McKenna duties, excluding motor cars, tofalled £1,000,000, compared with £580,000.—Reuter.

Brussels, June 15.—In an effort to solve the crisis which has deprived the country of a Cabinet for nearly three months, the King summoned a conference of the Catholic leaders Vaudevyvere, the Socialist Vandervelde and the Liberal Masson. He urged the subordination of party considerations to the need of forming stable government.—Reuter. INDIA'S LEAD.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. J. S. Wardlaw Milne (Conservative) with regard to conditions of labour in Japanese cotton mills at Osaka compared with mills at Bombay, Lord Winterton, Under Secretary of State for India, said he had been informed that the legal maximum working hours under the Japanese factory act were twelve a day but this need not be strictly adhered to in factories employing only male operatives over fifteen years of age. Women usually worked between 10 and 12 hours a day and were employed at night. The amendment act of 1921 reducing the legal maximum for women to eleven hours daily and prohibiting night work of women was not being enforced at present. The legal maxima in India were sixty hours a week, eleven daily for adults and six daily for children under fifteen years of age. Night work for women was prohibited.

headline: RAILWAY MAGNATE.
text:
The death has occurred of Mr. Julius Kruttschnitt, ex-Chairman of the Southern Pacific Railroad Company.

[Mr. Kruttschnitt, who was born in New Orleans in 1854, was connected with railways all his life, being resident engineer in charge of construction as far back as 1878 and rising to be General Manager of the Southern Pacific Company's Atlantic lines in 1885, ultimately becoming director and chairman of the whole concern. He was also a director of the Western Union Telegraph Company and similar concerns.]

headline: OUTLOOK GRAVER.
text:
The situation is unchanged. The removal of negotiations from Shanghai to Peking has not caused any outward excitement.

It is reported that the Japanese have handed in a Note of protest as regards the affair at Kiukiang; on June 18, but both the Chinese and Japanese authorities are maintaining complete secrecy.

The Union of Labour, Commerce and Education, which came into being in consequence, of the events of May 30, have decided to insist on the continuation of the strike of shops, despite the decision reached at the meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, which decided that the banks should re-open on Sunday.

headline: Terror Gang.
text:
The students yesterday terrorised the shopkeepers, bankers, and members of the Chamber of Commerce in connection with the decision to re-open the banks and shops to-day.

Two special meetings were held in the Chamber yesterday, at which the extremists contended that foreigners would view the re-opening as a sign of weakening. The business members pointed out that the closing of the banks and shops was not materially affecting the foreigners but was causing tremendous Chinese losses, instancing that enormous supplies of tea and cocoons were piling up in Shanghai, which were at present unfinanceable and not movable.

Yesterday morning the meeting resolved to postpone the opening until June 24. Last night's wholly rescinded the resolution of June 19, and resolved to postpone settlement day until the end of the lunar month, namely July 21.

headline: Chairman Attacked.
text:
During the discussions, the extremists bitterly attacked Yu Ya-ching, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, charging him with having received $500,000 from the Imperialists to re-open the banks and shops.

Yu Ya-ching vehemently denied this. He hurried to Shanghai from Peking, and since worked day and night in the interests of China and her people. He had not influenced the voting, and he had sufficient money for his few remaining years on this earth.

The attack on Yu Ya-ching silenced other solid business men, and the rescission was carried by a huge majority.

While a definite split between the business members, and the extremists has not occurred, each group is attempting to justify itself, and the outcome will depend largely on the attitude of the Chinese Government.

headline: More Bluster.
text: Delegates, representing 48 colleges, met at the Law College this morning. They sent a deputation to interview the Foreign Minister and War Minister, this afternoon, demanding severance of diplomatic relations with Britain and the impeachment of the Hankow Tupan. The situation, however, at least outwardly, is becoming quiet. There are no signs of the boycott or strike. Numerous students have left for their homes during the past week.

headline: Chungking Trouble.
text:
A message from Chungking yesterday, states that after student agitators worked up popular excitement, rioters on the 17th. attacked foreign customs, employés and assaulted Britons on the streets, though none were seriously hurt. Meanwhile a demonstration occurred at the British Consulate, where the rioters-threatened-the-consular Chinese stuff. The Consul, thereupon, requested the city commandant to furnish a consular guard and restore order. As there was no response, the Consul evacuated the Consulate and went aboard a gunboat.

He sent messages to all Britons, advising them quickly to assemble on the gunboat. The community, on June 18, found accommodation at the riverside, under the protection of gunboats where they are remaining. Order has

been restored in the city, but excitement has not subsided. It is unsafe for foreigners to appear in the streets, though no danger is apprehended under present circumstances. The British Consulate is damaged to an extent unknown, and troops are now guarding it. At Chungking, as at many other centres the rivalries of the militarists have proved an important factor in the situation. Leaders, who are inclined to restore order feared popular ill-will and held aloof at a critical period.

The Foreign Office Note, in reply to the Powers' note regarding the riots against foreign sentiment in China, states that the accounts of different incidents given therein are not in accord with the local Chinese authorities' reports.

The Note gives a lengthy Chinese version of the recent occurrences. It says the Hankow British Volunteers suddenly opened fire on an entirely unarmed crowd and the British authorities should assume full responsibility for their violent action.

At Kiukiang, during an altercation between the police and a small number of workmen, fire suddenly broke out at the Taiwan Bank. During the confusion at the time of putting out the fire slight damage was "caused" to sundry articles in the British and Japanese Consulates. Such damage was accidental. Regarding the killing of a British subject at Shanghai, the Note says that he was outside the Settlement, where the Municipality has built roads without China's consent. The motives of the criminals have not been ascertained. It is regrettable for the above reasons that the incident occurred.

headline: From Afar: EDINBURGH, June 20.
text:
Over a thousand delegates, representing sixty countries, attended the opening of the World Women's Christian Temperance Convention. The Conference opened with a devotional session, at which delegates from South Africa, Australia, Denmark Canada, India and China gave short addresses.

Miss Tinling from Shanghai said that in the present trouble the Chinese should not be blamed for the effects of Bolshevik influence. The rest of the world was threatened with the same changes. The Chinese were only doing what mobs do elsewhere.

headline: Shanghai Position.
text:
Shanghai is quiet, but there is no cessation of anti-foreigo propaganda. The decision to reopen the banks and shops is favourably affecting the general situation; but merely reflects the necessity of the Chinese to end the phase of the situation causing them much severer losses and inconvenience than foreigners.

The shipping strike, which is a strong anti-foreign weapon, is not weakening. Strikers are beginning to kidnap Japanese employees who are taken to Chapei, robbed and beaten and only released on payment of money and promises to quit employment.

A wireless from Chinkiang says the strikers have resolved that coal will not be sold to British or Japanese.

No danger is now apprehended t Anking.

At Swatow anti-foreign demonstrations continue.

At Foochow an anti-Japanese boycott has been decided upon but no date has been fixed.

Ample Strike Funds.

The extremists are not concerned in the deadlock, for sufficient funds for strike purposes continue to flow in from China and abroad.

The strikers' programme includes a huge demonstration in the native city to-morrow, which together with the growing activities of organised bands of ruffians, is giving rise to additional precautions. Chang Hsue Liang is bringing a second brigade to Shanghai of Fengtien soldiers and is taking up strategic positions in the vicinity of the native city.

The vernacular papers all published Mr. Chamberlain's speech, some commenting on it as nonsense, and others treating it impartially.

headline: Chungking Situation.
text:
The position here is improving. Foreigners are remaining across the river. The other Yangtze ports, and Peking and Tientsin are quiet. The Chinese Delegation has been ordered to Peking.

Message From The Pope.

The University professors recently solicited the Pope's support in the Shanghai affair. The Pope empowered Mon-signor Constantini, the Apostolic Delegate to China, to signify his sympathy with the great Chinese people and keenly deploring the shedding of fraternal blood and praying that concord and order would soon be restored in a spirit of mutual understanding, according to the principles of justice, equity, and Christian charity.

headline: Outroges Continue. SHANGHAI Tura
text:
The strikers yesterday afternoon attacked the wharf coolies coaling the Blue Funnel liner Pootung. Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's assistant compradore, intervening, aroused the ire of the strikers who set upon him and chased him to the river-side, where failing to reach a sampah, he fell in and was drowned.

A Briton, Mr. Moalem, a driver of the Volunteer Machine Gun Co., was going home in uniform last night by way of Lord Lane when he was struck between the shoulders and the neck with a meatchopper. He was seriously wounded and taken to Hospital.

[A message received later in correction of the foregoing states that it was the younger brother of the Holt's Wharf compradore who was killed, not Messrs. Butterfield & Swire's compradore]

No damage resulted from the wharf incident which was quickly over. A British warship is protecting the wharf to-day.

Mr. Moalem is progressing satisfactorily.

headline: KOWLOON WEDDING.
text:
The Rosary Church, Kowloon, was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday; the parties being Frederico Muria Gutierrez, only son of Mrs. Milvinin of Shanghai, and Margaret Frances, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Barnes of 3 Lyemun Villas, Kowloon.

The bride was given away by her father and was tastefully attired in white georgette with silver trimmings. Her two attendants the Misses Annie and Agnes' Barnes, wore dresses of mauve crepe morocain and pink crepe morocain respectively and the bride's mother was dressed in beige crepe morocain.

The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. Father G. M. Spada and Mr. A. A. R. Botelho and Mr. J. W. Barnes were the bridegroom's sponsors. Mr. O. Baptista was at the organ and suitable solos were rendered by Mr. E. G. Aquino.

The reception held at the Club de Recreio was largely attended and after receiving the congratulations there of many friends the happy couple left for Repulse Bay. Next week, they are to leave by the Empress of Asia for Shanghai.

Paris, June 21.—The "Petit Parisien's Berlin correspondent reports that the British Charge d'Affairs called on Herr Stresemann and emphasised the importance the British Government attaches to the proposals in the French note in regard to security. He declared the note formed the best possible starting point in the negotiations between Germany and the Allies.—Reuter.

Rome, June 20.—The Chamber by 274 votes to 42 adopted a Bill relating to the dismissal of State officials. The Minister of Justice said officials will be asked to embrace the Fascist faith. No official could feel offended, thereat. The law would only affect small groups of would-be politicians who infested the Ministries. An amendment to exclude magistrates from the scope of the law was defeated, Signor Mussolini declaring that the purification of all departments was imperative. No exceptions could be made.—Reuter.

headline: Santiago de Chile. June
text:
Santiago de Chile, June 21.—In order to stop Soviet propaganda in Chile the Government has ordered that the Russian ship Vorovsky shall not be allowed to enter Chilean ports.—Reuter's American Service.

Moecow, June 21.—The Russian Batic fleet made for the open sea this morning for manoeuvres, with Admiral Frunze abroad a battleship.

Paris, June 20. The Main announces 20 arrests in Paris and the provinces in pursuance of the measures of suppression of Communist propaganda in regard to Morocco. M. Painlevo will early raise a question in the Chamber raising Parliamentary immunity in respect to two Communist leaders, who are deputies, to enable prosecution.

Tangiers, June 20th—situation in the Western Spanish Zone is becoming serious. The Rif contingents are concentrating at various points along the Court Torcan Larache line.—Reuter.

headline: LIFE IN CHINA.
text:
MR. BALDWIN REVIEWS SITUATION

GERMANY AND THE LEAGUE.

Mr. Stanley Baldwin, the Premier, addressed fifty thousand Lancashire and Cheshire Unions at Lord Derby's residence at knowsley Park. He said that the host satisfactory feature of the foreign outlooks was the evident desire of Germany to continue negotiations with both Britain and France. He wished that Germany would enter the League of Nations very soon, when existing problems, notably disarmament, would assume a new and better aspect.

headline: OVERSEAS TRADE.
text: Mr. Baldwin continued that the chief factor in checking the growth of Britain's overseas trade was the great increase in productive and distributive costs. We were threatened with a conflict between the coal-owners and miners, each with a very strong case, but all the time the financial position of the industry was getting worse. These conflicts must be lifted on to a new plane by both masters and men. He hoped that the negotiations which were about to be resumed would result in carrying on an harassed industry over a year or two till it would be easier to negotiate permanent settlements.

headline: CHINA'S CHRONIC TROUBLE
text:
Discussing foreign affairs, Mr. Baldwin referred to the disunion and confusion in China, which amounted to little short of inarchy. Some of the unrest is somet候 from sources which, if not checked, will make the unrest chronic and anarchy universal. We have long been deeply interested in the prosperity of China. While we have profited by her prosperity we have contributed thereto materially. We have definite responsibilities for the security of British life and property in China, which we are determined to discharge with energy and firmness. It is our duty to have the unfortunate collision at Shanghai thoroughly investigated and see that impartial justice is done. It is impossible for us to deal with that incident by ourselves. We are in consultation with other nations to secure an agreement as to the best method of proceeding, but we must go further yet. WASHINGTON TREATY.

Mr. Baldwin said the Powers three years ago, agreed with China at Washington that efforts should be made to readjust some of the provisions of the old Treaties now out of date. Complications had incurred and both sides had drifted too long without action. "I am glad to say that the cause of the delay does not rest with us. The Washington Treaties have now been ratified. We shall be only too glad to appoint delegates to push on the work of the conference with China and discuss and settle the questions at issue when once the present unhappy incident is closed and normal conditions are restored. There should and will be no delay in considering, with sympathy and generosity, the legitimate requirements of China as regards the future conduct of the trade on her borders and the administration of those areas where our people enjoy the privilege and responsibilities of trade."

At a conference of the World Federation of Education, Association of Edinburgh yesterday, Scholars, Hums, speaking on belief of the Russimaches, declared that the East and West would never be united without Russian Association, Doctor Tai, Chancellor of the Peking University, said that China now clearly recognized that the regeneration of her ancient civilisation would be a reality if the rising generation could be educated on new lines.—Reuter.

headline: BOYCOTT DENIED. / SHANGHAI CHAMBER'S DESIRES
text:
SPEEDY SETTLEMENT

The Chinese General Chamber of Commerce denies that it has decided on a British and Japanese boycott.

The Chinese General Committee of Commerce has requested Reuter to deny the report in the local Press to the effect that the Vice-Chairman of the Chamber, at a meeting last Sunday, announced that goods purchased after June 30 from British and Japanese sources would be seized and confiscated after discovery by the students and that the boycott should be maintained for a year. The Chamber states that the report is unfounded, as the meeting was convened exclusively to discuss steps to urge the Chairman, Yu Yah-ching, not to retire. Hostile foreign criticisms have here been aroused and various retaliatory measures are proposed in letters to the foreign Press, all calculated to do harm to Chinese and foreign relations. This Chamber wishes all foreign business men to understand that no action of an illegal nature has been or will be contemplated by the Board of Directors, whose only hope is that a speedy settlement on the lines of international justice of the May 30 affair, may be effected and the moral support of the foreign friends of China abroad is earnestly solicited and will be heartily appreciated.

headline: Wharf Coolies Resume.
text: The majority of the wharf coolies have resumed. Many indignation meetings are being held as the result of the closing down of the Labour Unions. Agitators accused the Fengtien General of accepting foreign bribes. A female speaker endorsed the suggestion that efforts to compel the General to modify his policy should be made.

headline: RUBBER BOOM. / REQUEST TO MODIFY RESTRICTION.
text: A manifesto emphasising the adverse effect to their interests of the legislative restrictions of rubber exports from Malaya and Ceylon has been signed by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, the Royal Automobile Club, the Commercial Motor Users' Association, and the British Cycle and Motor Cycle Manufacturers' and Traders' Union. The manifesto points out the enormous increase in the prices of crude rubber for immediate delivery and says that approximately six million cycle and motor users in Britain are paying and will continue to pay the price during the present restriction; describes the scheme as too inelastic to adjust the supplies with the necessary rapidity to prevent the maintenance of an abnormal price, and urges that it is the Government's duty to modify the scheme.

headline: A NEW BURRIS.
text:
The first instalment of a series of hitherto unpublished letters written by the late Mr. Walter H. Page during his American Embassage in London, and now obtained from the private files of the late President Wilson, appears in the June issue of "The World."

In a letter dated February 22, 1914, Mr. Page declared that the feeling was strong in this country that the United States Government wished to prohibit European financial adventurers from exploiting Central and South America because we wish to exploit them ourselves!" "Men who have looked on at the parcelling out of the world and have taken part in it don't all at once think of the people that dwell on a land before they think of the land itself," the letter continued. "This is one interesting test of the great distance that the Old World thought is behind our thought in all matters of popular welfare. I am constantly surprised to discover how far ahead of them we have travelled.

"I told the German Ambassador (Prince Lichnowsky) here the other night that we wished no more territory, and didn't want Mexico as a (free gift of the gods. He looked at me—a mere glimpse of one one hundredth of a second—and I saw this flit across his mind: 'You are a consummate liar or an impossible idiot.' In this kingdom the Tories do not understand the vocabulary that the Liberals use, and the Liberals wouldn't understand our democratic vocabulary. They have no idea of our notion of freeing men."

HISTORIC THE GOVERNMENT. Writing on May 1, 1014, Mr. Page described a conversation which he had at dinner with "a remarkable old lady, the daughter of one earl and the wife of another," who was "full of the notion that a democracy was necessarily vulgar and venal." "This old Tory notion of the corruption of the United States," Mr. Page's letter proceeded, "crops up oftener than you would think, and there lurks in it a sort of aristocratic hope that it will yet fail. But this is not an active anti-American feeling. It is rather a social resentment of the success of a democratic order of society. It is, I am sure, becoming more and more merely a subject of historical-interest—a curious survival that has no important meaning now."

Of a conversation with a Welsh bishop, who spoke "with shame and grief and horror of the wicked effort to disestablish 'God's Holy Church' in Wales and thus strike the first blow, towards the dethronement of his most gracious Majesty himself, Mr. Page wrote: "I swear he almost persuaded me to be a Tory." He continued:

"When the appeal is made in the name of English history and of your vision of this conquering race sending its soldiers and sailors and bishops and adventurers to blazo ways for civilisation on all sens and continents, it was that sort of an appeal that almost persuaded me to be a 'Tory'—till I got out in the open air and drove over the bridge to Westminster Hall, where, at 11.30 at night, the political partners of the bishops were hectoring and insulting the Government in a way that ought to have put the Tower in commission again."

"They use this historic appeal—they use everything—to cling to their privileges, often you feel with all sincerity. They are English history; they are England; they are the Empire; and they point to all the strength and glory of the past to prove it—for all the world exactly as our own tariff nabobs used to point to every good thing in our land as of their bringing, and as Wall Street used to prove that the prosperity of Yuda Dam in Arizona was of Wall Street's creation."

Nobility not "played out." Here they are in many respects the finest flower of British civilisation. Physically they are remarkable. The noble families of this kingdom have practised engenies pretty well for centuries. Now and then there's a dirty duke's (I know one who is the biggest liar in England) now and then a noble lord marries a chos girl or gambles away his ancestral vectrals. But, after all, they are few.

"The race isn't degenerating: I imagine that the noblemen of this generation on this island include more first-class men than those of any preceding generation. The error they make is to conclude that they owe their vitality to their special privilages. headline: SHANGHAI APPROVES / MURDER DONE?
text:
SEQUEL TO HECTIC NIGHT.

HONGKONG'S FIGHTING STRIKE MEASURES.

SIMILAR POLICY REQUESTED:

MILLIONAIRE AND POLICEMAN.

The emergency measures adopted in Hongkong for dealing with strikers have aroused the ire of the Labourites at Home, but judging from editorial articles and the correspondence columns in the Shanghai newspapers, they are looked upon as the very thing for bringing the Chinese involved to their senses.

Donald Parsons, a millionaire member of the Stock Exchange, was celebrating so industriously amongst the cabarets that a policeman had to see him home.

Parsons invited the policeman inside, and the officer later retired with the members of the household, only to be awakened by the smell of smoke. He quickly phoned for firemen, who failed to arrive before Parsons and his son Vivian had been burned to death. The police are investigating what promises to become an amazing murder mystery, committed right under the policeman's eyes, even though they were closed.

"We adhere to our opinion that, if the strike can die a natural death, it had better be allowed to do so. If it can be broken by means of passive resistance, there will be the less heart-burning and bitterness afterwards. And if General Shing will act up to the threat of his own proclamations, put down the unions and suppress the intimidation, the workers would go back to their work with alacrity. Welcome news was received last night that he had caused six agitators to be arrested and there are other indications that his forbearance is reaching its limit. It needs only that he should shoot one intimidator, to make the rest understand that their game is up. But if he does not take action on resolute lines, then it will become necessary for the Settlement authorities to do so. Already it begins to be felt by persons in a position of responsibility that the strike and boycott can only be ended by a display of force. And if that line is reluctantly decided upon, there are plenty of ways in which it can be adopted. Why, for example, should the Settlement continue; by means of volunteer labour replacing the strikers, to supply water and light to Chapel, the headquarters of the strike? And why should the Chinese workmen who will not allow their fellows to work—every office probably knows whom it has to thank for this among its own former employees—be permitted to reside in the Settlement free to carry on their silent terrorization? As for those convicted in the Mixed Court, we cannot unfortunately use the "cat" but there are plenty of other more appropriate punishments for them, as Hongkong has shown.

The putting of agitators to "useful if unpleasant duties" in connection with the sanitation of the Colony has particularly met with approval as a fitting punishment, also the campaign conducted against intimidators and the banishment of idlers.

"One of our correspondents to day has obtained some extremely interesting information as regards Hongkong's way of dealing with strikers and intimidators, writes the North China Daily News." A good deal more might be told, but the censorship imposed in Hongkong is very strict and since the Government of the Colony does not wish to let out such information by the usual channels, we have no wish to defeat its policy by divulging what has been obtained from travellers. In a word, however, it may be said that the strike in Hongkong is being fought; not just played with; and the results of this were seen a day or two ago in the brief telegram saying that the volunteers for essential services had been demobilized, implying that regular labour was now available.

headline: CHINESE PROCLAMATIONS.
text: Simultaneously Mr. Arthur Sowerby returns to the charge with his demand for a forward policy, asking if we are still in the same mind as when a week ago we deprecated the line he wished to take. And yet another correspondent details a number of measures which might be taken to break the boycott. The answer to Mr. Sowerby is that a week ago things may have been different from what they are to-day. In point of fact they were. At that time it appeared that the strike funds were running out and that General Shing Shi-lien's proclamations might be expected to have an effect on the intimidators. With regard to the latter we have been waiting patiently. It is difficult to belliave that a man in General Shing's position can speak so plainly as he has done and not give effect to his words. Surely he must "lose face" by falling to do so to an extent far worse than any unpopularity he might earn with the riff-raff by acting sternly in defence of law and order. Nevertheless, the intimidation has grown daily worse, the strike funds have undoubtedly been replenished and the extreme party of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce is completely in the saddle.

headline: TENNIS EXPENSES / HOW JACOB WAS SUSPENDED.
text:
Light is shed on the vexed question of lawn tennis suspensions—briefly cabled by Iveuter—as a result of Helmore's team accepting hospitality from Pujols.

Writing on April 27, A. Wallis Myers, G. B. E., says: "Hochamptons spring meeting opened in fine but cold weather. The entry is of good quality, and includes Jagat Mohan Ead, who has just arrived in England to represent India in the Davis Cup. Moham Ead was to finalist at the All-India Championship, held at Alhababad, two months ago. He was better in that round by Mr. Andreae, who has also come." Davis-capping in Europe. Both have high reputations in their own country. Among other competitors are R. Iyccett (who won two rounds without ditheltry), A. A. Iycee, N. Mishra, Barclay, Hitchie, E. Higgs, and H. W. Austin, who is paired with Iyccett in the doubles. The ladies' charter is also good. Miss McKane is returning to open tournaments, pairing with her sister in the doubles.

Rochampton will lose the entry of 8: MJ Jacob, the present covered co-t champion. The Lawn Tennis Association have suspended Line from tournament competition in this country until further notice. A notification to that effect was conveyed to the executive at Roehampton. Mr. Jacob, who was on the ground, had not received personal notification of this decree. Mr. Jacob's suspension is the outcome of a breach of the amateur rule which apparently unwittingly he committed by joining a London team visiting Paris as far back as November last. The captain of this team had failed to obtain the necessary sanction from the Lawn Tennis Association, and his team accepted expenses from the Paris club, not only for their match, but for a subsequent tournament held on the same courts. This was contrary to the regulations; the offence has been admitted; it became a question of inflicting a penalty. The council suspended the captain of the team for twelve months. The other members were advised that they must agree to refund the proportion of their expenses paid by their hosts.

The negotiations were long. The I.T.A. claim that they have shown both justice and patience. I do not think that can be disputed. Yesterday's action against Mr. Jacob was taken, not, as I understand, because he disputed the commission of a technical offence; he held that his own association, the Association of All India, should be consulted as to the validity of the verdict. In other words, he wanted to appeal to another court. The I.T.A. claimed that they, and they alone, had jurisdiction in this matter, since Jacob proposed to play at their own tournaments, and he had admittedly (though not necessarily consciously) broken one of their regulations. They are unquestionably right. But I hope a way out will be found, and that Jacob's suspension may be withdrawn at the earliest possible moment. He has committed no offence which cannot be condoned by a frank admission of error. Nor are the council such "tyrants" that they would wish to deprive a former Davis Cup captain, who has taken up his residence in this country, of his desire to compete in our tournament, always provided their authority is admitted. I think that is essential for all players who compete in tournaments held under the sanction of the association. I would add that I found no evidence in support of the report published that the competitors at Roehampton were anxious to withdraw their entries in protest of the official action. A certain measure of sympathy was naturally expressed for Mr. Jacob, but it was felt that the matter was personal one between himself and the governing body. [Subsequently, Reuter, cabled that Jacob's and Fyzee's suspensions were withdrawn.]

headline: Local Honours.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail?

Sir.—The Hongkong's Honours list, is sadly akin to what the prevailing note in feminine fashions is said to be—slim. Does it tell us, in the words of Mr. Arnold Bennett "how the Government feels in its inside"—assuming that recommendations for Honours are made by the Government? Mr. Tanner gets an I.S.O. In addition to that well-merited recognition he is to be congratulated on the length of quiet but effective service he has been able to do in an exacting profession. For the rest—social workers, philantropists, commercial magnates, Government servants, and the people who do things and, blush to find themselves famous must wait. The Government "in its inside" feels that no one as yet has reached maturity. In Malaya they do these things differently. The Government's "inside" there is less liverish. It sees not as through a glass darkly. My fear is that this fact being known the exodus of the classes we have mentioned will become great; we shall have no reformers, no workers for good; no philantropists left to do the good things that find their own reward, which perhaps will be just as well. The bestowing of honours is perhaps veiled in mystery. Doubtless they were first given for doughty deeds. Up to quite recently they were also bestowed for "dough" by deeds; but they have been known to be given for services rendered by those with sufficient time on their hands. The system generally has been wrong—so much so that quite respectable gentlemen in such enlightened places as South Africa and Australia have definitely decided to refuse all honours. I have an open mind on the question. If anything I would do away with the system entirely unless the holders of Honours undertook to remain here all their lives. In its place I would have a temple of fame—something on the lines of the Temple of the 500 Geneii at Canton—wherein Tussaud-like representations of all those who have served the Colony well would be permanently housed. Here on at least one day in the year I would bring the school children of the place to rest their eyes and minds on the effigies of those who had done so much for so little without impairing their health. And any who called this the Hall of Pomposity would receive my severest rebuke. But after all I am of Cato's mind when he said: I had rather it should be asked why I had not a statue than why I had one.

headline: PRESIDENT POLK."
text:
ROUND. THE. WORLD. LINER

YESTERDAY'S RECEPTION

Operated by the Dollar Line free from the Shipping Board control, the s.s. President Polk could carry whatever-drinks the passengers might desire, but in accordance with the principles of the owners she is "dry" from choice.

As she lay at the wharf on the Kowloon side yesterday this liner was boarded by those interested in passenger traffic and in the local shipping world generally. The many improvements which have been effected on the ship since it was last in port were the subject of much comment.

Advantage has been taken of the opportunity afforded by the burning out of the boat at the disastrous fire at the New York wharves to re-model it entirely and this is particularly noticeable in regard to the utilising of space which had been devoted to hatchways for such purposes as a social hall, increased deck facilities and other comforts for the passengers, there being much increased accommodation.

As an all-round the-world-liner the President Polk has to be prepared for anything in the way of weather and this difficult problem has been met by the installation in the suite of radiators side by side with shower boths and all the cooling devices which the ingenuity of man can devise. All the cabins are roomy and fitted up with the latest improvements—mirrors at the back of cabin and cupboard doors being particularly of note. Everywhere there are odd corners where taps obligingly provide iced water aplenty. Again, there are covered walks for use in cold weather and plenty of open walking space when passengers experience such weather as Hongkong is providing them with at present. Everywhere there are ingeniously operated skylights which indicate the provision of supplies of cool and fresh air at the passengers' convenience.

Amongst those who yesterday afternoon made the acquaintance of the new ship and of Capt. Ahlin Mr. Charman, the purser, and Mr. E. L. Matteson, the general agent were Mr. Demester, head of the Java-China-Japan line, Mr. C. F. J. Quarles van Ufford, manager of the Hongkong branch of the Java-China-Japan Line, Mr. Y. Tsutsumi, Manager of the Tokyo Kisen-Kaisha, Mr. Featherstone of the Canadian Immigration Offices and Mr. T. H. Crapnell, of the Hongkong and Kowloon. Wharf and Godown Company.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE.
text:
TODAY'S HARLIER CABLE

The first trial was resumed in the Mixed Court to-day of seventeen rioters, twenty-nine forfeiting their bail. Lengthy evidence was taken all day long.

Mr. Harry Westridge, a China Inland Missionary, gave evidence that he witnessed occurrences on the afternoon of May 30, which he recounted in minute detail.

Asked whether he considered the shooting necessary, he replied that as a missionary he hated shooting, but if he had been the officer of the law responsible for the station which was attacked he would. There was no option. He believed there was no evidence to show that the students had any personal feeling against the police and vice versa.

Asked whose fault the shooting was, he replied that it was a misfortune. If the events related had happened in England the result would have been, the same. It was the students not the police who were looking for trouble.

Doctors Muir and Chen gave evidence that they examined the wounded and dead rioters. Their opinion was that the bullets entered the bodies from the front or obliquely. One body was hit in the back of the head. It is believed that he was killed at the New World Theatre on June 2. The case was remanded until to-morrow. Bail was offered to all the accused

headline: Chang Tso Lin's Attitude. PEKING. June 9
text: The vernacular papers report that Feng Yu-hsiang has issued a circular supporting the student agitations, also that he has wired to Chang Tso-lin urging that the militarists co-operate with each other and the people to obtain rights for the Chinese. Chang Tso-lin is reported to have replied agreeing with these sentiments, but it is believed that the General is merely desirous of showing sympathy with the popular movement and does not intend any anti-Foreign action.

headline: Settling Down
text:
Apart from the shipping strike, Shanghai continues to settle down. The bakers resumed work this morning. Some shops have reopened, and domestics are returning to work.

No riots have occurred in the river-ports but much unrest is reported. Women and children refugees from Kiukiang will arrive in Shanghai to-morrow. Consular reports from Chungking state that students are agilating, but two commanding Generals assure the Consuls that they will maintain order and guarantee the safety of foreigners.

H.M.S. Hawkins has put in at Woosung. Her departure for Singapore has been postponed indefinitely.

A. P. C. Offices Wrecked.

Rioters wrecked the offices of the Asiatic Petroleum Company at Taiyuanfu.

headline: Peking Student's Demands PEKING. June 0.
text:
The Students' Union here continues to pass extreme resolutions demanding inter alia that all ricsha 'collies' in the Legation quarter should strike, that Anglo-Japanese employed by the Government for Chinese firms should be dismissed, that the telegraph and water should be cut off from the Legation quarter, that the Government should despatch troops to Shanghai, and that Chinese should leave foreign employment.

So far there are no signs that any of these measures are being put into operation, and the suggested boycott also appears to be ineffective.

headline: A Japanese View.
text: The “Jiji” reports that at today's Ministerial Conference, Mr. Shidehara prophesied a worse development in the economic phase of the Shanghai situation, although the rioting is decreasing. The Cabinet agreed that a more practical step as regards the riots was impossible until the joint Investigation Committee's report was received.

headline: THE INTREPID LADY
text:
Next, America. America, intrepid lady, rides on a bison, with its head down; as if about to butt something. Another intrepid lady, one of America's daughters, is hitting the bison on the head with a nasty-looking stick. "I'll learn you to butt my mother!" she is saying. A man at her side has set down rather suddenly on an astonished lion, which he has completely flattened out. Its claws dangle helplessly in the air. Another standing lady, with a lamb's fleece over her shoulder, offers a bunch of, I think, rhubarb, to an indignant man in a hat and nearly nothing else, who is rightly refusing it. He is holding a rifle in readiness in case his wife offers him rhubarb any more.

Africa comes next. Egypt sensibly rides a camel, which, though possibly old-fashioned, is a far more reliable-steed than these new-fangled bulls and bisons. Near her is a wise man with a note-book in his hand, a kind of hassocky thing—or is it a bale of merchandise? And is his book the Precepts of Ptah-Hatep or a cash account book? Beside the camel a rather "school-marry" person shakes her, finger at a negro who is making faces at her behind Egypt's back. Don't do that, you naughty, rude boy!" she says severely, "after all the pains I've had educating you, too!"

And last, Asia. An elephant nearly as large as the lady who is seated on him has rather ignobly collapsed. You see it is not only the weight of his rider that oppresses him. There is a conquering young man with a far-away expression leaning against the elephant's ribs and sticking the point of his shield into the elephant's side, regardless of the pain he must be inflicting on that dumb, faithful creature. Round the other side a visionary is seated rupt in dreamy contemplation, with his foot very near the elephant's tail. I consider it a great tribute to the remarkable powers of concentration possessed by the visionary that he can retain that serene, placid expression with a justly irritated elephant well within kicking distance. I couldn't.

Homer, at the centre, touches his lyre, to which listen Dante, on the one hand, and Shakespeare, his tunic trimmed with the now fashionable row of buttons on the other. headline: QUIET SATURDAY.
text:
While any unrest which existed throughout the French Concession yesterday was due principally to the activities of unorganised loiterers and would-be looters, the condition to-day of the areas under foreign protection would suggest that even these had ceased all efforts to resist the determined resolve on the part of the authorities to maintain peace and order at all costs.

Like yesterday this morning opened quietly following an uneventful night. No incident to mar the present quiet situation presented itself at any point in the International or French Settlements throughout the forenoon and it is almost safe to predict that the rainfall which commenced this afternoon will have a staying effect upon any contemplated outbreak or demonstration scheduled to take place as part of the programme of the strike-leaders and anti-foreign propagandists.

Yesterday drew to a close with success, for the most part, on the side of the agitators. From all parts of the compass reports were received that additional labourers had joined the ranks of the idle. By nightfall the number of workers of all classes who had stopped work amounted to something over 200,000 and this number was swelled almost hourly. While this was to be deplored it was certainly gratifying to note that almost without an exceptional instance, the servants, labourers or professional employees who finally agreed to quit did so solely through intimidation. The activities of the strike leaders were broadcast and relentless. Backed up by misleading. Communist propaganda, ill-advice and distorted viewpoints acquired through contact with nationals and literature from countries which have sunk beneath the social plane through adopting similar methods, the local Bolsheviks yesterday pursued their programme of social and business upheaval throughout the length and breadth of the city.

Frenchtown Involved. As we reported in our last night's issue, Frenchtown succumbed to the agitators after having remained aloof from all disorders for a period of several days.

The same methods employed to bring about this condition as in the International Settlements though fortunately no blood was shed. Shopekeepers, market-vendors, public servants and houseboys were all approached in the same sly, menacing manner and in a great many departments the workers agreed to follow the instructions of the intimidators. Shops of all descriptions closed their doors as ordered but, with even an eye for business, pigeon-holes and side entrances remained open for the use of customers. The public services of the French Concession have not been as fiercely approached as those within the settlement.

Why They Must Go.

(North China Daily News.) Shanghai, June 6.

A number of our staff who lives in one of the smaller hotels, yesterday noon came across a very good example of the manner in which this strike is being managed. On his floor there is an ancient coolie, probably well over 77 years old, a typical specimen of the lower classes of old China, totally ignorant, but thoroughly imbued with the idea that in every hour of the day, without consideration for himself, he must obey implicitly every order of those he regards as born to be his superiors. At that he is a wonderful servant, most highly thought of by all the foreigners he tends. The old man was found packing up his few rags and his one ceremonial suit, and the dialogue that ensued is probably more expressive in the pidgin.

What thing, coolie? You no go?"

"Master, mississee, my now-wantches go. Every man stop. My can stop. Every man go, my must go." his work, yet thoroughly, intimidated with a threat which he believes in his pathetic ignorance can and will be carried out, but which the man who made it knows full well he could not carry out. And this case is typical of thousands.

headline: Obscene Propaganda.
text: The trial of the rioters is going on. Agitators are endeavouring to extend the shipping and commercial strike by means of circulars which they are distributing, and, which objectively attack individual Anglo-Japanese firms. These are commonly attributed to Chinese rivals.

headline: Cool Advice
text:
The students to-day are holding a monster demonstration and also compelling carts, ricshas, and other vehicles to carry anti-Foreign flags many of which are black-edged. They are also distributing anti-Foreign literature containing wildly extravagant statements declaring that the Shanghai affair is the most brutal and cold-blooded atrocity in human history.

The Waichiaopu last night requested the Italian Senior Minister to advise the Legations that their nationals would be wise to avoid to-day's demonstration.

It is understood that the Minister replied that if the Government had any doubts as to the outcome of the demonstration it should prohibit it.

headline: Polka Blamed
dateline: Tokyo, June 10. Kiot Trial. SHANGHAI, June 10.
text:
The Chinese Legation, instructed by Peking, this morning issued a statement blaming the foreign constables for firing without a warning. The statement denies any anti-alien or pro-Bolshevik complexion and accuses the Shanghai Municipal Council of traducing the friendly relations between China and the Powers to conceal its own faults.

At the trial to-day the American assessor announced the admissibility of documents containing Bolshevist Literature which the police seized at Shanghai University and which was not admitted yesterday.

Inspector Everson, who ordered the firing on May 30 described the circumstances and said that the crowd was absolutely uncontrollable for three minutes before the firing. The squad consisted of eleven Sikhs, twelve Chinese and two foreigners.

The Chinese Magistrate asked whether firing at the legs would have been effective.

Witness replied that such would be contrary to the instructions which were only to fire as a last resource and then to shoot to kill. He had to obey those orders. The defence called Sidney Anderson, an American Methodist missionary.

Witness said that he did not see any resistance either by the crowd or by the arrested men. The crowd were only blocking the street and cheering. They shouted something like "Hurrah" and were quite manageable. Their object was apparently a sympathetic movement in favour of the imprisoned students. He guessed that about fifty or a hundred shots were fired, and considered the police absolutely unjustified in firing.

Cross-examined, he said he could not see the people in front of the crowd at the time of the shooting. He could not understand what they were shouting. He admitted that the police were too few to hold back the crowd. Doctor Cline, a Methodist Missioner, and ex-President of Soochew University, gave evidence similar to Mr. Anderson's. The hearing was adjourned until tomorrow.

Dr. Cline is also an American. Seaman's Strike. SHANGHAI. June 10

The China Merchant's Steamship Company, a Chinese shipping concern, have suspended allings indefinitely. Some shipping companies are instructing their vessels at present at other ports not to return to Shanghai.

headline: LAOK ON GOVERNMENT PROVISION.
text:
The Director of Education was questioned at yesterday's Education Board meeting, over which he presided, as to the number of private schools that had been started in the Colony during recent years and members expressed the opinion that the Government was not doing as much as it might do in the matter of providing educational facilities for a growing population. Mr. Wylie criticised the Government in that there was only one Government School for Chinese in Kowloon.

The discussion arose out of answers to questions which Mr. Li Forster had given notice of, these being that 126 new private schools had been registered in the Colony during the last three years; that 103 had given up and that "the teachers at such schools were not forced to attain to a fixed standard.

There were schools of many types, said the Chairman referring to the absence of a fixed standard for teachers. Some of them were performing a very useful work while others only gave a smattering of education for the benefit of workmen or servants. The suitability of the teacher was, however, always considered before a school was admitted to registration and no Government grant was given before a certain standard of efficiency was attained. There was supervision of them by the Government at least once a year.

Mr. Alves asked what was being taught in the schools and Mr. Wylie replied that so far as the Department was concerned they had no means of telling. "I think," Mr. Wylie added, "these schools should be done away with altogether and that the Government should provide schools to take their places."

Mr. Forster said that it did seem on the face of it, that the Government had not made adequate educational provision during the last ten years, for the expansion of the Colony. His whole point in asking the questions was to show that these private schools had come into existence as a result of a demand which was not being met by the Government and he felt that perhaps they were exploiting the community. Several voluntary schools had gone in for expansion but the only development on the part of Government Schools appeared to be that in connection with Sayingpun School which would only supply sufficient places for the present scholars. Schools run by religious bodies were cheaper from the Government point of view than if they had to maintain them solely, and it might be that the Government was getting education too cheaply. The voluntary system was not adequate to deal with the situation and it was because of that these night schools had sprung up run on a commercial basis.

The Chairman remarked that the Government could not hope to provide sufficient schools to take the places of all the private schools and it would be a pity for voluntary effort entirely to be swamped.

Rev. T. W. Pearce attributed the present exceptional demand for schools to the troubled state of China resulting in people coming to Hongkong. Perhaps when China returned to normal again some of these difficulties would disappear.

Mr. Wylie congratulated Dr. Pearce on his optimism in expecting to see China return to normal again.

Rev. T. W. Pearce: It might certainly be a suitable subject for discussion. (Laughter).

Mr. Wylie asked questions relating to the provision or lack of provision of educational facilities for Kowloon in the course of the meeting. Was there any hope of the Government erecting more schools there at an early date? he asked.

The Chairman replied that he could not say definitely. They had sites for two more schools and he was hoping that sufficient money and labour would be available to make a start shortly.

Mr. Wylie pointed out that there was no Government Girls' School on the Peninsula. The only boys' school, too, was at Yaumadi and even at that distance they were having to turn pupils away. The meeting closed with a reference by Mr. Wylie to the technical classes in Kowloon. Could the Chairman give any information regarding them?

The Chairman said that he had not received the report in time and it had not yet been circulated.
