A few hours later, a breadman employed by Hall and Holtz was stopped at the same place, and relieved of 12 loaves of bread.

Although the thieves in both these cases took the articles to the Chinese Fire Station, officers on duty there, who were interviewed by members of the Municipal Police, denied all knowledge of the incidents.

A number of students tried to seize 20 cattle which were on their way to the French Slaughter House, but desisted on the approach of a party of naval men who escorted the cattle to the settlement.

A Reuter telegram from Peking of June 14. says:—

"General Feng Yu-hsiang, interviewed by the "Ching Pao," declared that in case of hostilities against Britain he would be the first in the field. He said that China need not fear England, which had a big Navy but only a small Army."

We do not for a moment suppose General Feng ever said such a thing, but the invention is interesting, remarks the "North China Daily News."

A “North China Daily News” correspondent writing from Chetoo on June 8 says: — I will just mention that the situation is not so pleasant. The Chinese are demonstrating. They are marching through the streets by hundreds, carrying banners and shouting: “Kill the foreigner,” etc. So far no damage has been done to foreign property but no one knows what the situation will be to-morrow. I did my work all day among some Chinese firms and did some fairly good business. I called on a few foreign firms but had very few results. They seem to be worried about the present disturbance and it is indeed difficult to talk business to men when their attention is attracted by shouting mobs in the street: There has been no violence to foreigners as yet but the police told me to go inside when a mob of ruffians passed by. I think that patrols may be sent ashore from the American men-of-war to-night and if so perhaps the day will be quiet.

headline: Hankow Quiet.
parent_headline: MAKING MISCHIEEF. / STUDENT AGITATORS URGE BOYCOTT. HANKOW HOTBED.
text:
A feature of the local situation, which remains quiet, is the unchecked publication of grossly misrepresented reports regarding Shanghai and other places by the Chinese papers.

Two students have arrived here from Shanghai. Their intentions include an attempt to promote a boycott.

About ten student agitators have also arrived from Peking.

An interview between the Consular Body and Tupan Esaio Yao-nun is being held this afternoon.

Negotiations Break Down. Shonechai Turns 14

The breakdown of the negotiations between the Commission sent by the interested Powers and the Chinese delegates is explained by a subsequent communiqué shewing that the Chinese insisted on dealing with a series of demands not directly connected with the recent outbreaks at the same time as the incidents themselves with which the Commission is only authorised to deal. The Commission consequently decided to return to Peking, whither the whole question now goes back.

(On Saturday evening Reuter's Agency issued the following official communiqué:—

"Since there has been a considerable easing of the local situation during the past three days, instructions have been given for the withdrawal from duty of a portion of the defence forces and these instructions have already been carried out."

[Of course this means no relaxation of the defence and watchfulness.]

Shanghai presented an almost normal appearance on Saturday in that most of the shops in various parts of the Settlement, including Nanking Road were open to some extent, if not entirely, for business. The markets, which have been a point of attack on the part of the agitators and students, were open, with the exception of the meat shops—flowers and garden produce could be seen everywhere, at Hongkew also.

At Arts and Craft all workmen, 450 in number, have resumed their labours, while at Kelly & Walsh's western plant none have returned. Of the Settlement laundrymen, no less than 1,500 refuse to work.

Numerous instances of thieving and rice snatching took place during the week end. On Saturday a gang of coolies assailed two wheelbarrows on Dalny Road and made off with 30 bags of rice. In the Wayside district another gang made off with one sack.

A party of Chinese, who appeared to be students, took 17 bottles, of which 10 were full of milk, from a coolie in Jessfield

headline: STAR THEATRE. / TREAT FOR MUSIC LOVERS.
text:
The enterprisag management of the Star Theatre has engaged two artistes of world-wide repute who will appear for one night only—on Sunday next. These are Modle Lena Ambiose, soprano and Senor Scamuzzi, late of the Italian Grand opera company. Both are well known in the Colony. Middle Ambiose has a Soprano voice of delightful sweetness, range, and clarity. Scamuzzi—is Scamuzzi! This artist caused a furore on each of his appearances. He has not only a voice but a personality. The mind wanders to "The Barber of Seville," "Carmen," and "Rigoletto" when thinking of Scamuzzi. Both artistes will render selections from Grand opera. There is sure to be a great welcome awaiting these two incomparable artistes.

According to this morning's Chinese papers, the "China News," (the vernacular paper which was raided by the Police some days ago and has since suspended publication) is to be republished by permission of the authorities.

Three Chinese were remanded for one week when charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy yesterday with the alleged murder of another Chinese at Wongneichong village. The body of the murdered man was discovered by some coolies below the filter beds on June 1.

headline: FLASH OF FLAME. / STRANGE STORM HEAR CANTON.
text:
TWO LIVES LOST.

FOREIGNERS' NARROW ESCAPE

A whirlwind of intense velocity lasting only two minutes or so struck Tungshan and Taishatau (to the ef the Canton) about 10 45 last night, causing considerable damage and the death of two men by electrocution.

Huts and matsheds were carried away and a part of the German Consulate roof was torn off. Trees were uprooted and the sky was suddenly illuminated by a big red flare. Electric wires snapped, causing the two men's deaths. Foreign residents who had just got back to their homes in this district were reading about the Hongkong storm when many were thrown violently about while windows came tumbling down. It is felt that if the phenomenon had lasted longer much havoc would have been wrought. The strange part about it is that Canton proper were entirely unaware of the sudden storm.

Canton is generally quiet although rumours of a general strike on Monday are in the air. Minor fighting is reported from Fatshan and the North River.

Ngai Bong-ping's resignation is attributed to disagreement with General Hsu Shung-chi and, so the story goes, to some troops lent him by General Leung Hung kai having been disarmed at the hour of victory; by Cantonese colleagues. The latter report is totally unconfirmed.

H. E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs) will inaugurate the new building of St. Joseph's College on June 24 at 5.30 p.m.

Tokyo, June 18.—The Nichl Nichi reports that the Japanese Construction Company started work on the Taonan Taitahbar� fallway last month and expected to complete it in October—Rentor.

headline: THE RIGHT WAY.
text:
CRITICAL SITUATION CONTROLLED.

GOVERNOR'S FIRM DEALING

On the morning of June 1, just as the students and labour unions of Changsha were preparing for their annual demonstration connection with the "Six-One" (June 1) movement, when it was proposed to commemorate and make demands in connection with the anniversary of the unfortunate affair on the Bund here in 1923 when marines from a Japanese gunboat, in their effort to clear the dock of a violent mob and permit the landing of passengers and freight from a steamer of the Nisshin Kaisha, shot into the crowd and killed a man, the news came to hand of the serious rioting on May 30, in Shanghai, writes a "North China Daily News" correspondent. News that the police had fired into the crowd and that nine students had died caused tremendous consternation and a great outburst of nationalistic feeling. Processions were started at once and for a day or two Governor Chao made no attempt to repress them.

headline: EXCITEMENT HIGH.
text:
By June 4, when word had come of later disturbances in Shanghai and of further shooting, the excitement was running fairly high. Schools that had been parading the streets in connection with the June first celebration now held meetings—that is, the Student Unions did—and other meetings of a violent sort were called in the hall of the Educational Association.

The leaders of the movement calling for retaliation soon organized what is to be called "The Tsing-Hu. (Tsingtao-Shanghai) Cruel Killing Snow Shame (Vengeance) Association." Included in the leadership of this organization are students and labour leaders as well. Every sort of radical proposition has been made, most of them copying the proposals made in Shanghai, for death penalties on the officers that did the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, for the removal of British consular officers; for a complete boycott against the British and Japanese; etc. In many of the schools agitated meetings have been held, usually ending in the taking of a solemn oath by the students body to work here after body, soul and spirit, for the sake of China; and for the enforcement of a complete and permanent economic boycott against Britain and Japan.

headline: AMERICA DRAGGED IN.
text:
Those who watched these developments in school after school came to believe that it would not be long before other countries would be mentioned by name and included in the attack. By the morning of June 6, when word came of an incident in Shanghai on June 3, when American volunteers were fired upon near the New World Theatre, and police action had again become necessary America was also proclaimed as one of the nations to be found guilty. The telegrams here all said that the American Troop had opened fire with a machine gun and had "killed numberless persons." All sors of rumours of impending violence then spread over the city. The governor had already, on June 4, put up a strong proclamation, condemning the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, as unhumanitarian, but urging students and all others to refrain from acts of violence, so as not to give the foreigners any opportunity for incrimination and for retaliatory acts. He proposed severe measures for those who should be found disturbing law and order. This proclamation had had a decided effect until the afternoon of June 6, when the news of the American volunteers reached Changsha.

Before long a girl was found at the gate of the Educational Association, weeping and calling attention to a printed poster on the walls, soon put up all over the city to the effect that an engineer, a foreigner, in the employ of the Canton-Hankow railway, had beaten a Chinese to death. Later in the evening a new rumour was started to the effect that another foreigner had killed a Chinese to the west of the city.

The Governor, Incensed at these fabrications of disturbing rumours came out early on the morning of June 9, with a strong proclamation, showing that such statements were false and urging the populace to become quiet. The entire city was in a state of siege on Saturday night, with groups of armed soldiers guarding all the roads, in and out of the city. Word has come that on the night of Saturday. June 6, a mass meeting of labourers was held in the cotton mill on the opposite bank of the river from Changsha city. mission institutions, "have been taunted on the streets and called foreign slaves. At the same time, it must be frankly stated that, considering the provocdtion," the steadiness and loyalty of the students in mission institutions has been remarkable. They have tried to stand by and keep order and to refrain from joining in noisy demonstrations.

If the officials continue to keep a grip on things, the situation will surely quiet down soon. The Governor, usually giving the impression of being a watchful waiter, has been aggressive and definite, both in statement and action.

After a week of increasing tension in Changsha, ending with a very serious threatening of evil and the fabrication of numberless rumours on the 6th of June, Governor Chao Heng-ti showed himself to be thoroughly master of the situation. He has been governor for several years and has usually been deemed a mild man. Two years ago he caused commotion among the ranks of labour agitators by executing two student leaders, famed for their violence in speech and manner, who were found to be inciting the workers of the cotton mill to revolution.

His next vigorous display of power came late on Saturday evening the sixth. Learning of a vast mob that had gone out to surround the railway yards, apparently to get even with an engineer about whom a false rumour has, been started during the afternoon, he sent out a large detachment of soldiers to cut off the mob. As they met, the mob taunted them and there was some bandying of words until the soldiers slipped cartridge clips into their rifles and told the crowd to go. This shut down the trouble.

On Sunday the sixth, Governor Chao called together a large and representative group to the yamen and made them a long address. First gaining the car of the company by expressing deep sympathy for those who had lost their lives in Shanghai, he went on to speak of the disturbances here in Changsha. "What influence," he asked, "can we have in telegraphing counsel to other provinces if we are unable to keep order here in Hunan? When people know that in the west of Hunan, at Shenchow, at Hungkiang and elsewhere bandits over-run the country, how can they pay attention to our words? How can we help others when such a situation arises as arose yesterday (June 6) when the fabricat on of rumours and threats of evil. compelled Yali College (the college of Yale in China) and the Fu Hsiang School (a Union Mission Girls' Middle School) to shut down? The interference with order reached such a pitch yesterday that if I had not put on the severest martial law orders, no one knows what would have happened later on at that time."

At a later point in his speech the Governor said, "We must watch and keep order lest, as a lesser ro-sult, we have another outburst, similar to what occurred in Boxer year; and lest, as a major result, we find China broken up and her integrity destroyed"

Such words from a Governor of Hunan are strong. Usually pride does not permit the criticism of local conditions. But Governor Chao came forward at the emergency and saved what was a very ugly threat from maturing.

headline: CITY WELL CONTROLLED.
text: As I write today, June 8, things seem calm and the city is well in hand. As the Governor intimated so many student agitators were calling for strikes and for leaving class duty, that the authorities of the College of Yale in China felt their only course to be to close the institution promptly. The annual Commencement exercises which were set for June 23 will be of a simple form, it is said, with less of the academic formality than usual. Other schools which were closed up during most of the week between June 1 and 6 got under way again today, the Bin. They should be able to keep going till the end of the term if no new word of trouble comes from Shanghai.

Union Church was yesterday the scene of the wedding of Miss Eva Iona Aber, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Aber of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and the Rev. G. Newbern, missionary, of Cheung Chau Island, only son of Mr. and Mrs. William Newbern, of Pitman, New Jersey.

The bride was attended by Mrs. J. Olen as matron of honour and wore a white satin crepe dress trimmed with embroidery and tulle veil. She carried a bouquet of white roses. The matron of honour wore a white organdle dress over pink silk and carried a bouquet of pink roses.

The ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. H. Johnstone and the best man was the Rev. J. J. Olen.

headline: STRIKE EXTENDS.
text: It should be noted that for convenience sake all meals at the Hotel are being served in the grill room and that they are of the very best. To-day, at tiffin an air of cheerfulness pervaded the room, aided at times by the band. Mrs. Taggart and others were prominent and the Hotel is to be complimented on what it is doing.

headline: Exodus: Continues.
text:
Long before sunrise, in fact within a short time of the incoming river steamers discharging their passengers, hundreds of Chinese had swarmed on to the wharves determined to obtain a passage for Canton or the native village. At daylight this morning the vessels due to leave this evening were absolutely full of passengers. Little or no cargo was worked, but a constant stream of men and women, all carrying luggage, were turned back. A conservative estimate places the number shut-out at 10,000. Many of those going down were domestic' servants, ostensibly from foreign households.

This morning some households still had their servants and were able to get their meals, but the majority of the more fortunate employers were informed that their employees would, reluctantly, as in nearly every case, have to leave about tiffin time.

headline: Scouts Helping
text: The Hongkong Boy Scout's Association is doing its "bit" and arrangements in hand by which this help will be considerably extended if necessary. At present there are several qualified Scouts working in hospitals and many others are holding themselves in readiness for all sorts of other work, down to working in lifts if necessary. The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave, Commissioner, informed us on enquiry that all Scouts had been asked to report to Headquarters. The parade arranged to take place at Government House on Wednesday had been cancelled.

headline: Rumours About To-morrow.
text:
Many are the rumours about tomorrow. Those who correctly predicted on Saturday night that the trams would stop on Sunday now say that the beef and other stalls at the market may have to shut down tomorrow and that the engineeringers and firemen on harbour ferries may stay away.

Vernacular papers suspended publication this morning but extras were issued.

Hundreds of workers are crossing the Territories to travel by train to Canton, A China Mail reporter was informed that had it not been for the rain yesterday and to-day, a much larger number would have trekked miles but refrained for fear of weiting their personal effects.

headline: Earlier Developments.
text:
The strike which commenced on Friday has now developed considerably and affects all classes and almost all industries and businesses.

The boys at the Peak Hotel began to leave shortly before tiffin on Saturday and the remainder went after tiffin. The exodus, from the Peak Club took place on Saturday afternoon, but this did not interfere with the dance in the evening, refreshments being served and the necessary washing-up done with skill and dexterity, by the members themselves.

The Chinese staff at Repulse Bay did not leave until tiffin on Sunday. It was stated that between four and five hundred Chinese engaged in the two hotels—the Peak Hotel and the Repulse Bay Hotel—had gone. A few of the boys from the Hongkong Hotel left during the course of yesterday morning, and last night all but one or two had left. At all the hotels, however, careful and well-planned arrangements have been made to "carry on" as well as is possible in the circumstances.

The boys began to leave the houses in the Peak district on Sunday morning. Previously there had been no suggestion of a strike.

During the night, however, the following notice, in Chinese, was stated to have been left at a considerable number of residences:—

Gentlemen,— I his is to inform you that in consequence of the recent incidents in Shanghai, causing workers and students to suffer cruel deaths, our corps has determined to carry out a general strike on and from Sunday next. Anybody who fails to join the strike will get from our corps extraordinary treatment.

This precious document is said to have been found on the doorsteps of the houses early in the morning. Its effect was extraordinary.

When the employees of the Tramway Company finished their work at Saturday mid-night, there was no reference to any possibility of a strike. The drivers and conductors, however, failed to put in an appearance on Sunday morning and consequently yesterday no trams were running.

At the tiffin given in honour of H.E. the Governor at the Hongkong Club on Saturday, His Excellency made a passing reference to the possibility of his approaching departure being postponed on account of the strike. "If this nonsense continues," H.E. declared, "I am going to see it through, and I do not think the arrangement will be a comfortable one for those responsible for my delay." In view of the developments, since this speech was delivered it seems highly improbable that H.E. the Governor will leave on Saturday as arranged.

headline: Further Details.
text:
About 11.30 a.m. to-day, a Japanese was shot near the French Bridge by an unknown person who is said to be a Chinese. Two shots were heard. One bullet went through the man's left arm into his body and the other struck his leg. He was carried into the Concession by French sailors and Dr. Reynolds of Shameen. Later on I was informed that the man had succumbed and that he was connected with the Japanese hospital at Nam Kwan.

All the Hongkong and Macao boats to-day were anchored off Shameen with the exception of the s.s. Charles Hardouin. The Honam did not sail for Hongkong this morning and is anchored in the same place.

The Canton Government has issued an order that all former gambling houses and Yunnanese holdings are to be used as strike quarters and that the merchants are to contribute to strike funds.

Although the Chinese employees on Shameen have declared that they do not wish to strike but it seems that they will ultimately yield to the inevitable.

What the World is Being Told. Below will be found the Reuter messages broadcast from Hong- kong:—

The motormen and conductors of the electric Tramway Company have struck. The service is temporarily suspended. The strike of Chinese servants is spreading. Many boarding houses, some hospitals and hotels are affected. Boy Scouts are mobilising for the purpose of assisting the hospital. The Government has offered a reward of $250 for information leading to arrest and conviction of persons endeavouring to disturb the peace of the Colony. Numbers of Chinese are leaving the city for Canton. Chinese crews on several more British steamers have deserted.

The Volunteers have been mobilised. Boy Scouts have replaced the striking Chinese attendants at Hospital. Six steamers of the Indo-China Navigation Company are tied up.

Later.

A number of British and other foreign women and children have arrived from Shameen whence they were advised to leave. Police re patrolling the business quarters of Shameen precautionarily.

headline: Canton Shooting.
text:
An unknown Chinese shot dead Mr. Nakadai, the Japanese treasurer of the Japanese Hospital, just outside Shameen, and carried off a bag with five thousand dollars with which Mr. Nakadai was returning from the Bank of Taiwan.

The Japanese Consul has strongly protested to the local authorities, reserving the right to claim indemnity, and asking for police to be posted outside Shameen. He advised Japanese subjects in Canton to come to Shameen.

Many foreigners are going to Hongkong.—Most of the others residing outside the European quarter are now coming to Shameen.

The strike at Shameen began this morning. The Chinese are (ielty leaving the Concession.

There are no disturbances. British Marines are operating the ice-plant and are ready to operate the waterworks.

Later.

The Civil Governor of Canton has requested the merchants to contribute to strike funds. Gambling houses closed before the war have been taken over as quarters for strikers who number approximately 1,500. Shameen has an extra supply of food. Another Japanese destroyer has arrived.

headline: COLLEGE BAZAAR.
text:
In spite of adverse circumstances the faith of the promoters of St. Stephen's College Bazaar in carrying on with the arrangements was justified and the Building fund will benefit considerably as a result. The Bazaar concluded on Saturday afternoon and evening. At three o'clock Sir Henry Pollock, K.O., who was accompanied by Lady Pollock and Miss Middleton Smith, introduced in the Great Hall Mrs. Chow Shou-son and spoke of the keen interest she had always taken in the welfare of St. Stephen's. Mrs. Chow Shou-son acknowledged through Mr. Li Chor-chi and in opening the Bazaar wished it and the Building Fund every success. Mrs. Chow Shou-son was then presented with a memento of the occasion by Mr. Chan Cheung-nin, who has been largely responsible for the general arrangements of the Bazaar. The Rev. H. W. Hewitt, Principal of the College, thanked Mrs. Chow Shou-son both for her presence and the interest she had always taken in St. Stephen's. He would also take the opportunity of thanking all who had worked toward the success of the undertaking and had given unsparingly of their time and labour.

The outdoor entertainments were the same as had proved such an attraction the day previously and they drew another large crowd in spite of the heat. The stalls in the Great Hall were also extensively patronised and the appearance of the Colony's champion ping pong players in a specially arranged tournament for a cup was the signal for a general rush to the room in which it was held.

In the evening a variety entertainment and cinema show were given to a large "house."

headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, June 2, 1925.
text:
To-day's news from Shanghai is only reassuring to the extent that it emphasises the determination of the Police and the Municipal authorities to subdue the disturbances at all costs. Within a few hours the vapourings of a few students of Communist tendencies have been responsible for the creation of an international crisis which may drift along a course diametrically opposite to that intended by the first few demonstrations.

Not even the best friend of China would desire a replica of the Boxer Riots and of the humiliation that these eventually brought in their wake for China. But hot-headed youth inspired by sources that know not lav and order—and in fact are "up against" it—cannot be expected to stop and think of the consequences. But at the same time they themselves must share the suffering of these consequences. They cannot expect sympathy. They cannot be raised to the status of martyrs. Law and order must prevail even in China when the lives and the interests of foreigners are menaced.

It matters not at this distance from the scene of conflict whether the riots originated in the killing of a Chinese workman by a Japanese during the recent-cotton strike, or whether the primary cause was a desire on the part of Chinese students to escape examinations and get promotion without them. What does matter, and matter very much, is the fact that the rioters have shown their hands by the inflammatory posters they have issued broadcast over the city denouncing Imperialism and foreigners. That is proof positive that they have only been waiting for the flimiest excuse to break out of bounds and foment what really is tantamount to an anti-foreign rebellion. That is both a stupid and a dangerous policy to pursue. It must recoil on the heads of the Chinese themselves and on the Chinese as a nation.

If those who have the authority and the influence do not step into the breach and assist the Municipal authorities and the Police in Shanghai in the speedy restoration of order, they will assuredly regret it. There must be no weak-kneed measures or sentiment. The riots must be quelled and the originators and participants severely punished. And if that is not done within a reasonable space of time the duty of the British and the other foreigners whose interests are menaced is obvious.

The growing amount of motor traffic is revealed by the amendment of traffic regulations published in the last number of the Government Gazette. Seldom, if ever, does one see a truck in charge of a number of screeching men. The Government has wisely initiated or encouraged a system of motor haulage in keeping with modern conditions. This is all to the good and a further aid to safety, for it is admitted that proffemoving vehicles are less a danger to traffic than the slow moving kind. The speed of 15 miles and 12 miles per hour assigned to various trucks is reasonable. What is of vast importance to the efficiency with which the road haulage is used. The additions covering ordinary vehicles are sane. A licensed driver is not to allow his vehicle to be driven by one who is unlicensed; whilst public motor vehicles are to carry a spare wheel and a serviceable kit of tools to the satisfaction of the head of the police. There should, it appears to us, be some rule covering those roads where there is either no sidewalk for pedestrians, or one of narrow dimensions making it almost impossible for it to be used. In this class of thoroughfare the pedestrian is in extreme danger of injury. A word of caution to drivers should not be out of place.

headline: HONGKONG AND THE CHATER COLLECTION.
text:
Reviewing the Chatter Collection: A Catalogue of Pictures Relating to China, Hongkong, and Macao, 1655-1860," with descriptive letterpress by James Orange (Thornton Butterworth. £7.7s.), Mr. J. O. P. Bland writes as follows in the "Sunday Times," (London): Of the many benefits conferred by Sir Paul Chatter on his fellow-citizens of the Crown Colony of Hongkong, assuredly none will rank higher in times to come than his gift of this collection of pictures and books descriptive of the early days of the Colony and commemorative of the events which led, and the men who contributed, to its making. This handsome volume, with its eighteen plates in colour and 243 in half-tone, constitutes a very fitting and felicitous monument, not only to the public-spirited munificence of "Sir Paul," but to the memory of the stout-hearted mariners, pro-Consuls, and merchant adventurers of England who, against heavy odds, opened up new and great highways of commerce in the Far East. It contains, moreover, much more than the customary catalogue of an art collection, for Mr. Orange has done his work as editor and commentator with a through knowledge and enjoyment of his subject and much scholarly discrimination. The arrangement of the work, in appropriate sections provided with exhaustive indices, should make it of real and permanent value to students, while the numerous quotations from contemporary authors, which accompany each section, enable the casual reader to form a very vivid and accurate impression of the events and scenes they describe.

It is a wonderful pageant of stirring days and captains courageous which these pictures present, beginning with the earliest attempts of the Portuguese Spaniards, British, and Dutch in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries to secure a footing for trude on the coasts of southern China, and to penetrate beyond the barriers of the Celestial Empire's splendid isolation. After the entry upon the scene of the stately orgosies of the Honourable East India Company, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, the European figures in the pageant become conspicuously British. This was to be expected, for, from 1678 onwards, when the Company established its direct and regular trade with Canton, Amoy, and (Later) Chusan, the long and often disbearing task of opening up commercial relations between China and the rest of the world—of sowing, where others have since helped fall almost entirely upon England.

The movement derives an extra importance from the identity of the commander, who will doubtless personally report the Shanghai situation to his father. It is also believed that Chang Tso-lin is taking advantage of the situation to strengthen his grip on the Shanghai region.

The students' efforts to cause general strike failed owing to official precautions

headline: INCIDENT OF THE FLAGS.
text:
A circular has been issued by Mr. E. C. Lobenstine, Secretary of the Council of Higher Education of the Chinese Christian Educational Association, reviewing the outbreak from the Christian viewpoint, containing a warning against coming to erroneous conclusions before the result of the enquiry is known, and enclosing a statement by Dr. Potts on the closing of St. John's University.

The students who took the chief part in the demonstration of Saturday, May 30, came from four radical colleges, two of these were the Shanghai University control of the student movement. Within the last two or three days, largely owing to the valuable work done by the Young Men's Christian Association, a change has taken place within the Student Union and every effort is being made to keep the more conservative element in control of the Union's activities. The Union is coming out in opposition to the use of force, although still active in the promotion of a general strike. The strike situation is serious and is growing. Foreign nations have brought in marines who are assisting the regular volunteers and those who have volunteered for temporary service.

The students are still in Shanghai College although they are not attending classes. The faculty of the College passed two resolutions the day before yesterday; one lamenting the events of May 30 and the other calling for a thorough investigation of the entire situation.

It seems to us here that the present is a time when all in Church and Christian institutions need to exercise the utmost caution when careless remarks may, because of the present tense feelings, be unduly magnified and receive wide publicity. One incident from an institution in another city is being widely circulated here, namely, that a foreign professor said the institution was supported by foreigners and therefore was a foreign institution and that if students did not like the way the institution was run the thing to do was for them to leave it.

The issues at stake in this incident are very far-reaching indeed, and raise for us, as Christian workers in China, fundamental questions both to our own Christian attitude toward justice and fair dealing and our methods of working in a country where there may justly be differences of opinion as to what course of action a Christian should choose.

We trust that the information that a thorough investigation is assured will be helpful to you in dealing with your own students and will help to convince them that the best thing for them to do is to continue with their studies, believing that the solution of the questions at issue can best be worked out by those who have access to all the facts, and that the publication of the exact facts is the surest first step toward securing strict justice.

President's Statement.

The President of the St. John's University, in his statement in regard to the sudden closing of the term; gives a brief chronicle of the events leading up to the present situation, in which he says:—

Owing to the excitement caused by the killing of some students by the municipal police in the riot on Saturday afternoon, May 30, an organization called the Students Union was formed by the student body at St. John's. A communication was received from this organization asking that the students might be allowed to suspend their studies indefinitely and also containing the following clause:—

"During the period of suspension, it is our express desire to make sure that no student is unnecessarily absent from the campus. For this reason, we beg to request you to refer all letters to us that are from the students parents or guardians asking for leave. We have a special committee to attend to this matter."

A joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held on Monday evening, June 1, and it was decided to appoint six members of the faculty (three Chinese and three foreign) to meet with six members of the student body (four elected from the College and two elected from the Middle School) for a conference. This conference was held on Tuesday morning, and an endeavour was made to get the students' point of view. Another joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held at seven o'clock (Tuesday). The faculty then adopted the following regulation:

The University has decided to allow the students to suspend their studies until next Monday morning 7.40 a.m. If at the end of that period, they are not ready to resume their regular duties, the University will be closed and all students will be requested to return to their homes. Students living in the vicinity are allowed to return to their homes now. “Letters will be sent to parents and guardians informing them that the University disclaims any responsibility for the students' welfare or safety while they are off the premises.” Students remaining on the grounds and occupying the College dormitories will be expected to observe the regulations put on by the administration.

Chinese flag could be flown at half mast. As it was late, the President had no time to confer with anyone and gave the permission. On Wednesday morning two flags were raised on the flag poles, the Chinese flag at half mast on one pole and the American flag at the top of the other pole. Bishop Graves requested that the flags be taken down, giving his reason that the flying of the Chinese flag at half mast indicated that as an institution we considered the action of the municipal police to have been wrong, which we were not prepared to do. The President promised to comply with his request and sent for the Assistant Scoutmaster. Owing to the fact that the Assistant Scoutmaster did not come immediately, the President decided to take down the flags himself which he proceeded to do. Both flags were taken down at the same time. When the students came out from their mass meeting which they were holding in the Assembly Hall they were surprised to find that the flags were down and sent a deputation to wait on the President to ask why they had been lowered. The President informed them that he himself had lowered them and that owing to the objection made to their being raised, he thought it was better to follow the rule which had been made by the Administration that flags would only be raised when the College was in session. A short time afterwards, hearing a commotion he went out from his office and found some of the students about to raise another Chinese flag. No permission had been asked for doing this and no expiration had been given to him. It seemed to him that it implied that the student body was in such a state of excitement that it was unwilling to abide by the regulations. One of the conditions upon which they were allowed to remain in residence while suspending their studies was that they would observe the regulations put out by the administration.

The President came to the conclusion that the only way to avoid conflict with the students was to close the institution for the term, and it will not be re-opened until next September. The students were not expelled. No threats were used, but they were requested to return to their homes.

headline: Faithful Servants.
text:
On Saturday morning a full shift of workmen returned to the Wing On Cotton Mill on Seoul Road after three days' holiday. They were permitted to work throughout the day and at six o'clock the management paid them off—not to return until further notice.

The tramway company is still getting a full quota of men, all but half-a-dozen returning daily to their labour. An attempt was made yesterday to resume the service on Chekiang Road which was discontinued after last Monday's riots, but the threatening crowds forced Chinese passengers to descend and the service has since been cut out. Rome has for long been recognized as the city of fountains. These are always playing, and give the city a gay and lively aspect. At almost every corner, especially in the ancient part of the town, you are bound to find one, and their number has increased to such an extent that the claim that modern Rome has surpassed imperial Rome, at least where fountains are concerned, is fully justified. Besides the large and well-known fountains, such as the Trevi Fountain, or the Fontana delle Naiadi, or the one at the Janiculum, there are numberless smaller fountains in various parts of the city which are scarcely ever visited by foreigners and the very existence of which is even ignored by many Romans. Many of these are really gems of art, hidden in remote and obscure corners in zones now mostly inhabited by people of the poorer classes.

headline: GENERAL.
text:
Says an Australian paper:—An unprecedentedly long record of service in the overseas trade with Australia is shared by the steamers Taiyuan and Changsha, which have been voyaging continuously between China and Japan and Melbourne via Sydney for close on 40 years. The first worn-out cable in the Melbourne Tramway system was taken by the Taiyuan to Hongkong at an early stage of her career, the broken strands being converted by Chinese into nails for use in tea chests.

What must have been an amusing spectacle, though productive of a certain amount of anxiety, occurred recently in the Mersey River. A hopper with a crew of nine men was blown on to a sandbank during a high gale. A lifeboat put out and stood by the hopper till the crew decided that it was no place for them. They were taken off and tugs remained by the hopper to take her off at high tide. But this hopper was of an independent turn of mind and slipping off the sandbank she made for home—which was the Sandon Dock. On her way she passed no fewer than fifteen ships, wending her way across the bows of one and under the stern of another. The tugs which had been ready to tow her off had nothing to do but follow her. As she arrived opposite her dock gates, which were open at high water, onlookers thought she was going to bump into the dock wall, but avoiding this she sailed serenely into her own dock, where human beings once more took charge of her and tied her up at her berth.

headline: PRISONER'S STORY.
text:
Mencia Carniciu presented a striking figure when she appeared before the Chief of Police to be examined. She is 26 years old and is the daughter of one of the richest families in Macedonia. She is a young woman of extraordinary beauty, tall and svelte, with jet back hair and blazing black eyes. She was utterly defiant in face of the murder charge. She told the examining magistrate she vowed two years ago to take the life of Todor Dimitroff as retribution for the lives of two Macedonian patriots whom, she declared. Dimitroff betrayed to their death, Telling the story quietly and proudly, she related how she came to Vienna and contrived, through a woman who knew the Dimitroff's, to arrange the exact seating for both parties in the Municipal Theatre for the performance of Ibsen's "Peer Gynt." Deliberately she told how she had visited the theatre and witnessed the performance earlier in order to judge the best moment to open fire.

"I knew he was always expecting attack, and always ready to attack, Mencis Carniciu declared," So I schemed to sit behind him, and as soon as the chance was right I fired"

Apparently Madame Dimitroff threw herself between her husband and the line of fire at the crack of the revolver, which explained how the second bullet found its mark in the skull of the dead man's wife. Dimitroff's companion, a man named Bagatinoff, had just been able to get his pistol from his pocket when Mencia fired again, killing Dimitroff.

The murder occurred at the moment when Peer Gynt was supposed to be drowned in the Sea. The Viennese actor, Herr Tressler, who was playing the part, emerged from the waves and came back to life, and addressed the audience from the stage, urging them to remain in their seats.

Police investigation establishes the political character of the dramatic murder. From the history of his past activities in Balkan politics the police have confirmed that Dimitroff was responsible for the death of two Macedonian leaders, Boris Sarafoff and Ivan Garbanoff, in Sofia seventeen years ago. Dimitroff, who was 50 years old, had been living in Vienna during the past few months at the apartments of a prominent Macedonian patriot, Philip Attanasoff, but the latter was recently driven from Vienna by the police. Recognised as a sworn enemy of the present Bulgarian Prime Minister, M. Zankoff, Dimitroff went in fear of his life. He was always accompanied by three or four Macedonians armed with automatic pistols, ready to protect him from assassins.

According to a number of Mencia Carnici's friends, an element of mystery in the case is now presenting itself. Her intimate friends declare she was madly in love with the man she killed. When the police arrested her immediately after the tragic murder she had a smoking pistol in one hand and a razor in the other. She admitted that she intended to commit suicide, but she was either too stunned or had no time in which to do it.

In the files of the Vienna police head-quarters officials have found an old Bulgarian extradition paper drawn up against Dimitroff, charging him with being a member of the Macedonian Revolutionary Committee.

The victim of the tragedy in the Burgtheater has now been ascertained to be the notorious Todor Panitza, the founder and leader of the Macedonian Federalist organisation, who twenty years ago murdered two leaders of the Macedonian movement, Sarafoff and Garbanoff in the streets of Sofia. Panitza then fled to the mountains in the Macedonian regions of Bulgaria, where he organised revolutionary bands and lived like a prince, though he was always in dread of assassination. He came to Vienna a few days before to adjust differences which had arisen between Bulgarian emigrants there. He was always attended by heavily armed companions to guard him against attack and murder, and his presence occasioned much irritation in Austrian political circles, which represent such abuse of the rights of asylum being extended to Bulgarian emigrants.

headline: “BEE BRAND”
text:
"There is no question that the old adage, 'early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy,' even if it does not make him wealthy and wise," said the Metropolitan Officer of Health, Dr. Purdy, endorsing the view reported in the cablegram. Dr. Purdy is an old friend of Sir Thomas Horder, and endorses the latter's opinion. "The modern prevalence of neurasthenia," he said, "is undoubtedly due to the bustle. G.B.S. ON CHURCHES.

WAS

of city life. In Sydney, the noise from the trams alone must induce a considerable amount of nervous disturbance. People should lead soldier lives, and eat simple foods, especially fresh foods, containing vitamins, such as lettuce, white cabbage, tomatoes, and fruits. Dr. Purdy added that, with care, there was no reason why people in a modern city should not live to 70, but the difference between city life and the simple life in the country was instanced by statistics relating to Massachusetts, which showed that the average life of agriculturalists was 68 years as compared with 30 for women employer in factories.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / SOME HOSPITAL EXPERIENCES.
text:
Phil Scott, the English heavy-weight boxer, in the opinion of the secretary of the Middlesex Hospital, "one of the finest specimens of manhood in the country," acted recently as a model for the anatomy class at the hospital. He was also the subject of a number of medical tests. His costume consisted of a pair of boxing shorts. He stood on a table in the theatre like class-room, very much as a model would pose for an artist. With his body tanned a light mahogany shade, and with the muscles rippling beneath a satin-like skin, he looked as fit as it is possible for an athlete to be. "A minor edition of Hercules" and "a muscular Apollo" were two of the descriptions applied to Scott by the students.

Armed with a long pointer, the professor indicated the points which he was describing by touching them with his wand as a teacher in a geography class indicates points on a map.

The two central figures were a curiously contrasted couple—Scott big and powerful and the professor small and looking very scholarly in his eye-glasses and long white operating gown. Scott fell into the different poses with perfect self-possession. Often he appeared very much like a figure in a Parthenon Frieze. A grim little touch was provided by the bones which lay on the tall desk behind the table. During most of the time the lecturer stood clutching one in his left hand—seeming to draw some inspiration from its "feel."

A certain amount of dry humour relieved the lecture. Once in demonstrating the muscles of the arm, the professor, commenting on the fact that one was not well marked, said in a matter of fact tone. "With all due deference to this gentleman I have better marked muscles than he has."

This was received by the students with roars of laughter and cheers. Scott afterwards said that he quite enjoyed the experience. "It was very interesting," he said, "and I have picked up certain little things in anatomy which will help me in boxing.

"I have had two courses of first-aid training," so I followed a little of what was being explained."

"The professor remarked on certain of my muscles not being well marked, but, of course, these are intentionally covered in fat for protection in the ring."

After the demonstration to the students, Scott went through many of the hospital departments and underwent a number of examinations. His blood pressure, breathing and eye-sight were all tested, and various "reactions" recorded. One of the tests included a sprint round the hospital garden.

headline: Motley The Only Wear.
text:
Smart clothes in the great world of London are quite, quite done for the daytime, to the distress, I suppose, of the more gaudy dress designers and to the makers of silks and satins and embroideries. Even for a very formal lunch, or for that now rather rare thing, a sea party, people wear glorified golf clothes (writes Viola Tree in the "Evening Standard.") There is limitless field for greys and browns and for accessories like stockings and handkerchiefs and belts to contrast and to harmonise. But gone are my dear black charmeuse and the charming Russian embroiders of yester year. A straight blue serge can be helped out with a frill, but honestly it is not really the way to dress. A helmet hat rammed on the head and a loose coat over a few other knitted coats in the smartest, and tailor-mades, rather severt, are worn by the young with their high-collared sweaters like jolly Jack Tars. They look nice, but so very, very hot, one tight sleeve over another. Extravagant lingerie is not barred, but it must never show with sports clothes—a shoulder strap or a piece of creeping filet would be absolutely fatal to the ensemble. Everyone to her taste, but where is the fun of the moors and marshes country if one goes about London just the same, looking as if one had a gun concealed under the elbow? Love Romance of a Nm.

A romantic love affair of a nun is reported from Bergamo, on the Swiss-Italian frontier. An old and wealthy Italian woman who was suffering from an incurable disease, and knew that she had not long to live, asked the Mother Superior of a neighbouring Catholic convent to send her a nun daily in order to read the Bible and pray with her. A pretty nun twenty-three years of age was chosen for the purpose, and during her daily visits frequently met the woman's sob, an officer in the Navy, and the couple fell in love with each other. The officer proposed marriage, and was supported by his mother. The nun, who was in a terrible dilemma, as she had to choose between her love and vows, recently confessed her "crime" to the Mother Superior, who took a lenient view of the affair. "Child," she said, "remain in your cell as a week and carefully examine her demands of your heart and con science, some vows, and then tell me your decision." The marriage will take place shortly.

headline: Clock Sota.
text:
A little clock in a black china case decorated with roses and with two tall vases to match, describes one of the many clock-sets that are now shown: (points out the "Manchester Guardian.") Generally speaking, these sets are cheap, of no particular value, but they are well designed and do not look out of place in a room. Once upon a time the marble mantelpiece carried a heavy clock, and usually two plunging horses as well, but there is no place, perhaps fortunately, for such things on the modern wopden mantelpiece; so the clock-set has been designed to fill the gap. To some extent, the china clock is a revival of an old fashion. Fifty years ago many of them rivalled the gilt figure clocks made in France, but the new clock sets have little in common with these elaborate old-fashioned timepieces, being quite simple in design and colouring, and, of course, very much smaller.
